title: The Mercy Ball
logline: On the night he’s supposed to be crowned heir to a Texas oil-and-cattle dynasty, Whit Ransome hides from his own coronation — and finds he isn’t the only one hiding.

cast.name: Amon Augustus Ransome
cast.role: Your father; chairman and CEO, Ransome Energy

cast.name: Lorna Whitaker Ransome
cast.role: Your mother; your father’s first wife

cast.name: Bunny Ashworth
cast.role: Chair of the Mercy Ball committee

dossier.text: Twenty-five. From Odessa. Married your father eleven months ago. He proposed nine weeks after she took $412,000 off him at a card table in the back room of the Petroleum Club in Midland. Fort Worth’s favorite joke: he lost to her at cards and married her to get his money back. Bunny Ashworth calls her “the Pigeon.” The ranch hands call her la Paloma.

Your wife. Born in Midland; SMU Law. Formerly a senior partner at Brightline Strategies, a Dallas crisis-PR firm. Now Chief Strategy Advisor to the Family Office, which is unpaid and absolute. Says “Mm.” when she’s filing something.
Five. Kindergarten in Fort Worth. Pink boots with everything. Facts about horses and sharks. Wants a retired pony named Biscuit more than anything in the world.

Seventy-six. Chairman and CEO of Ransome Energy (NYSE: RNSM) and general partner of Ransome Family Holdings, which keeps the family’s 52% of the vote. Has worn the same silverbelly Stetson since 1974; it has been replaced eleven times. Everyone expects him to name you his heir tonight.
Your sister, thirty-seven. COO. Wharton MBA. Can rope, cut cattle and pull a calf at 3 a.m. Wall Street’s preferred successor. Calls you “Golden.”
Ranch manager of the Mercy since 1991. Your father’s right hand. Taught you to ride; taught June to say “whoa.” Calls you “Bud.”
Your mother. Married your father in 1987; divorced in 2009. Highland Park, two museum boards, eleven years sober. Her name is still on the library in Pardee. Still in the will.
Your cousin, twenty-eight; your late Uncle Boyd’s son. Runs @RanchRoyaltyColt (2.1 million followers). Launched Mercy Ranch Water. Lives in a converted grain silo on the ranch.
June’s nanny for three years. From El Paso. Studying for the LSAT at night.
Founder and CEO of Halcyon Compute, a California AI company. Your father’s guest of honor tonight.
Texas Agriculture Commissioner, running for an open U.S. Senate seat. Slogan: RIDE FOR THE BRAND. Brought his horse.
Founder of Teague Permian Partners; host of the podcast Barrels & Bibles. Calls everyone “brother.” Not on the guest list. Never on the guest list.
Chairs the Mercy Ball committee. Married to board member Pete Ashworth. Says “bless” the way other people say “gotcha.”
Pastor of Lone Star Cathedral in Midland. Blesses pipelines on camera.

endCard.tag: In Texas, whoever owns what’s underneath can do almost anything to whoever owns the top.

s01.slug: INT. THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY — NIGHT
body: At 9:02 p.m. on the night he is supposed to be crowned, Whitaker Ransome is hiding in a church.

He stands at the altar step of the Chapel at the Mercy with his tie undone and a can of Mercy Ranch Water sweating in his left hand. The can is his cousin Colt’s product — “made with San Isidro spring water,” $9.99 a four-pack, a cartoon longhorn in aviators on the side — and at the moment it is one part San Isidro spring water to two parts the flask in his breast pocket. In his right hand are three index cards gone soft at the corners from his thumb. Six hundred yards east, the Mercy Ball comes through the cedar walls as bass, a steel guitar, and now and then the whoop of a man who has paid twenty-five thousand dollars for a table and intends to be heard from it.

The chapel seats a hundred and twenty and tonight seats one. Only the pin lights over the altar are on; the back half of the room goes down into dark like the deep end of a pool. It smells of lemon oil, cedar and the ghost of last weekend’s lilies. In the pew rack nearest him a glossy brochure promises “A Hill Country Feeling, West Texas Soul” at thirty-eight thousand dollars a weekend, linens extra. Whit has always liked the brochure. It is the most honest document on the ranch.

He squares the cards and clears his throat. Greer’s notes run down the margin of card one in her small upright hand: gratitude, legacy, the next Texas, one self-deprecating line. Under that, underlined twice: NO MORE THAN ONE. It’s the closest thing to a love letter his wife has written him since the wedding, and he means that nicely.

“Thank you all for being here,” he tells the empty pews. “I know some of you drove in from Dallas, and I want you to know — we see your sacrifice.” He leaves room for the laugh. He leaves room for the gratitude, which Greer says must feel unrehearsed and which he has now rehearsed nine times. “A hundred years ago, my great-grandfather stood on this land and—” And what. Looked at it. Wanted it. Greer has written STEWARDSHIP beside that line and circled it, which means it isn’t optional.

Somewhere in the stewardship he notices where his feet are. This exact square of polished cedar, under this exact pin light, is where he stood in May of 2019 and married Greer Talmadge in front of everyone who mattered and a photographer from Texas Monthly. He was sweating then too. “Here’s the thing,” he tells a hundred and twenty empty seats. “Last time I stood up here, I promised to love and honor a Ransome institution for the rest of my life. And that one’s going great.” The seats take it under advisement.

His parents built the chapel in 2003 on the site of the old stock pens and put their names on a brass plaque by the door, as if God might otherwise lose track. His father comes out here sometimes, alone, and always sits in the back, like a man in a waiting room who doesn’t want his name called. Whit has never asked why. In his family you don’t ask a man why he sits where he sits. You just don’t sit there.

Card two. This is the good one. He lifts the can to the rafters. “And I just want to say — I have waited for this night longer than Dallas has waited for a Super Bowl.” He holds for the laugh. The chapel holds it with him, politely, the way you hold a door for someone who turns out to be going the other way. Out in the dark a horse whinnies. Best review he’s had all week.
From the back pew, from the dark, a woman’s voice says: “It’s better without the joke about the Cowboys.”

He nearly drops the can. Mercy Ranch Water slops over his knuckles onto the cedar, and Mercy Events LLC will bill somebody for that. He knows the voice before he finds the face. Low, unhurried, the Permian still under the vowels. Everybody in Texas knows that voice. Everybody has heard it say almost nothing at a party.

She’s in the last pew, where the pin lights give out. Paloma Pruett Ransome: twenty-five, his father’s wife of eleven months, the card girl from Odessa who took four hundred and twelve thousand dollars off Amon Ransome in one night in the back room of the Petroleum Club, and got a proposal out of him nine weeks later. Bunny Ashworth calls her the Pigeon, and Fort Worth thinks that’s the funniest thing it has ever heard. Whit has stood near her at a dozen events — a christening, two funerals, the Stock Show, a Thanksgiving at which she ate pie and nothing else — and said “Hey there” to her at every one, in the voice he uses on donors’ wives and other people’s dogs. They have never had a conversation.

Black column dress, nothing on it. A turquoise cuff on one wrist; on the other, a man’s steel watch, too big, sliding to the bone when she moves. Her shoes — black satin, eleven hundred dollars, the kind that pinch at every one of them — are lined up side by side just inside the back door, heels to the wall, as if this were somebody’s house and she’d been raised right. She doesn’t get up. Something small and red walks over her knuckles, finger to finger, and back.

“How long have you been back there?” he says. “Who’s it for?” “Sorry?” “The toast.” The red thing stops on her middle knuckle. “Who are you saying it to? Because it isn’t them.” She tips her head east, toward the roar.

“Listen—” Whit says, which is what he says when he hasn’t decided what to say. He looks down at the cards. Card three is the one he hasn’t practiced. In his own handwriting it reads: Thank you, Dad, for — and then nothing, crossed out twice, as if the nothing had been wrong too. He has been trying to finish that sentence since August. He sets the card face down on the front pew, gently, as if it might finish itself while nobody’s watching, and turns to face his father’s wife.
“What are you doing out here?” “What are you?” It isn’t a dodge, exactly. She sounds as if she actually wants to know, which at the Mercy Ball counts as indecent exposure.

choices.text: Make it a joke. ‘I was told this room had great acoustics and no relatives.’
choices.ledger: You met your father’s wife in the chapel and made it a bit.
response: “Honestly? I was told this room had great acoustics and no relatives.” He points up at the rafters, then down the aisle at her. “Acoustics check out. I’ll have to take the rest up with management.”

She enjoys it. He can see her enjoy it: something loosens at one corner of her mouth, and the chip stops moving. Then, with exactly the same pleasure, she names it. “You’re doing the thing where you’re charming at me.” A small nod: a judge’s nod at a clean cut. “It’s very good. It’s like watching a man tap-dance in a house fire.”
He laughs, because she’s right, and because it has been years since anyone told him what he was doing instead of clapping for it.

choices.text: Tell her the truth. You’re hiding.
choices.ledger: You told Paloma you were hiding from your own party.
response: The acoustics line is right there. It’s a good one. Instead he hears himself say, “I’m hiding.” He lifts the cards an inch, as evidence. “From my own party. Which I think is a first, even for this family.”

She looks at him long enough that he starts to regret it. Then: “Okay.” She slides six inches down the back pew, away from the aisle, leaving room. From her, he suspects, that’s practically an embrace.
“Me too,” she says. “From a different party. Same tent.”

choices.text: ‘Mrs. Ransome.’ Button the jacket. Be the son.
choices.ledger: You called her Mrs. Ransome in an empty church.
response: He does up the button of his jacket, which is what Ransome men do instead of standing up straighter. “Mrs. Ransome.” He gives it the full Fort Worth: warm, correct, an inch of distance built in like a cattle guard.

“Mr. Ransome.” Exactly as cool, exactly as correct. She looks at the button, then at his loose tie, then at the button again. Then, not unkindly: “You can button it all the way. I’ve seen the rest of the family. It doesn’t help.”

s02.slug: INT. THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY — CONTINUOUS

body.text: She plays, and she plays fast. He tells her the pews are original Ransome cedar; she says she assumed so, they creak like the family. He takes a small bow at the altar step and she calls him “Mr. Acoustics” — once, and then never again, as if a nickname were a chip she only bets one time. It’s been a while since anybody kept up with him. It has been longer since anybody got there first.

“What are you hiding from?” she asks. Then she does something nobody else at the Mercy Ball will do tonight: she waits for the answer. He gives her the short version — the toast, the tent, six hundred people who have paid to watch him be grateful — and she listens to all of it with her chin on her fist on the pew back, as if it were interesting. That unsettles him more than flirting would. He can flirt in his sleep. He has, at least twice.

She calls him Mr. Ransome. She calls him Mr. Ransome when he asks if the music is too loud back there, and Mr. Ransome when he offers her the can, and Mr. Ransome in a tone that makes the name sound like a coat she’s holding out for him to put on. He lasts three exchanges. “Paloma—” he says, and she lets the word sit there between them, his, not to be taken back, and he knows he has lost something small and fair.

body: He comes halfway down the aisle and stops at the sixth pew, where the light runs out, and sits sideways on it with his arm along the back, like a man at a ballgame. She stays where she is. “The acoustics are better up front,” he says. “I like it back here.” She doesn’t say why. He’s beginning to notice that she doesn’t say anything for free.

“So. The toast. Be honest, I’m told I can take it.” “It’s good,” she says. “It’s very good. Except the parts that are you.” “Which parts are me?” “The pauses. You stop after every line like you’re waiting for somebody to tell you it’s allowed.” She turns the chip. “I’ve sat across from a lot of men telling a table what they’re about to do. The ones who mean it don’t wait.”

“Why aren’t you out there?” It comes out more honestly than he meant it to. It’s her party too; she married it. “Everyone at this party has already decided what I am.” She says it with no self-pity at all. “It saves me so much time.” “They’re not all—” he starts, and stops, because Bunny Ashworth is out there, and Bunny is, in every way that counts, all.

“Twenty-five thousand dollars a table,” she says, “to teach rural children to read. And they’ve hollowed out the books to put cactus in them.” “Succulents,” Whit says. “Greer would want me to say succulents.” “Is there a difference?” “About forty dollars a pot.” He saw the mockups in April. A leather Moby-Dick with an echeveria planted where the whale used to be. Nobody on the committee said a word. Neither did he.

She looks past him toward the door, where the brass plaque catches a little of the pin light: THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY · TO THE GLORY OF GOD AND IN THANKSGIVING FOR THIS LAND · AMON & LORNA RANSOME · MMIII. “Were you here when they built it?”

“I was, what — nine? Ten?” He squints, actually trying. “I remember cement trucks. A lot of cement trucks. Honestly, I don’t remember that year at all. It’s like a skipped track.” He shrugs. “Fourth grade. Rough year for everybody.”

She doesn’t laugh. The chip stops on her knuckle and stays there, and the only thing moving in the back of the chapel is the second hand on the too-big watch. Nobody wants to hear about a rich kid’s fourth grade, he figures.

He changes the subject. He nods at her hand. “What is that?” The chip starts moving again — index, middle, ring, little, and back — the way other people crack their knuckles. She holds it up to the light: red clay, worn pale at the rim, a derrick stamped in the center. “Petroleum Club. Five thousand.” A small pause. “Your father’s.” “He’s going to want that back.” “He’s had eleven months to ask.”

She closes it in her fist. “Let’s do something. One true thing for one true thing.” “Like truth or dare.” “No dares. Just the truth part. And not a fact.” The fist opens; the chip is gone, then back. “Facts are cheap. Everybody in your family has a thousand facts. I want a true thing.”

dossier.text: Turns a worn red clay poker chip over her knuckles — Petroleum Club, $5,000. Sits in the back pew. Wouldn’t come up the aisle.

choices.text: Tell her the true thing: you’re afraid he’ll pick you.
choices.ledger: You told Paloma you were afraid your father would choose you.
response: He means to tell her about the polo scar. He hears himself say, “I’m afraid he’ll pick me.” Then, because it’s out and lying there on the cedar between them: “Everybody thinks I’m scared he won’t. I’ve been scared he will since I was twelve. If he picks me, I have to be it. There’s no back door on that.”

She takes it seriously. She doesn’t tell him he’ll be wonderful, which is what Greer would say, or that he’s being a baby, which is what Hadley would say. She just takes it, like something handed to her that turns out heavier than it looked.

“Okay,” she says. “Mine.” She looks at the altar, not at him. “I came in here because it’s the only quiet building on two hundred thousand acres. I stayed because you were bad at this.” The chip turns once. “I liked watching.”

choices.text: Give her a true thing that isn’t the true thing. The polo scar.
choices.ledger: You told Paloma how you got the scar. She asked for something else.
response: “True thing.” He touches the scar through his left eyebrow, the one a photographer once said made him look like a senator who’d been in a fight. “Deerfield, junior year. Polo. A kid from Greenwich named Tad took a full swing at the ball and got me instead. Eleven stitches. Tad still sends a Christmas card every year. It’s always a picture of a boat.” He has told it at forty dinners. It has never once failed.

“That’s a fact,” she says. “I asked for a true thing.” “It’s a very true fact.” “Okay.” She pays him in exactly the same coin, without any rancor at all. “I was born in Odessa.” “Everybody knows that.” She tilts her head. “See how it feels?”

choices.text: Make her go first.
choices.ledger: Paloma went first. You still owe her one true thing.
response: “Ladies first,” he says. “It’s the Texas way. Also I’d like to see how it’s done.”
“Okay.” No hesitation; she has been dealt worse. She looks straight at him and says it plainly, like turning a card face up: “I’m not here for your father’s money.”

He laughs. Anybody would; half of Fort Worth would pay to have been in the room for that one. “Bunny’s going to need a minute,” he says. She doesn’t laugh. She waits for him to finish, patiently, and when he has, she says, “Your turn.” He opens his mouth.

s03.slug: EXT. THE SOUTH LAWN — THE MERCY BALL TENT — NIGHT
body: His phone buzzes against his ribs. Greer: “Where are you. Your father is on at 9:30. You are on at 9:40. Agenda: smile.” No question marks. His wife doesn’t use them in writing. She says they read as need.

body.text: Paloma is already up and collecting her shoes, two fingers hooked through the heel straps. It’s 9:14. “You owe me,” she says. “I’m good for it.” “Nobody in your family is good for it.” At the door she looks back once. “Count to a hundred before you come out. People talk.” “About what?” “Whatever’s cheapest.” And she goes out barefoot into the dark, the shoes swinging from her hand, and he’s alone in a church with a debt he can’t remember agreeing to.
body.else: Paloma is already up and collecting her shoes, two fingers hooked through the heel straps. It’s 9:14. “Count to a hundred before you come out,” she says. “People talk.” “About what?” “Whatever’s cheapest.” And she goes out the back door barefoot into the dark, the shoes swinging from her hand, and the door eases shut behind her on its pneumatic arm, and he is alone in a church again with a can of spiked spring water and nobody to perform for.

body: He counts to a hundred. He gets to sixty-one, which for a Ransome is a long time to do what a woman says, and at 9:17 he’s out the back door and walking east across six hundred yards of dark toward the light. At 9:20 he comes in through the west flap of the tent, re-tying his tie with one hand and re-assembling his face with the rest of him: eyebrows up a quarter-inch, shoulders down, the smile loaded and ready. It’s a face that photographs as trustworthy. It has never once let him down, which isn’t the same as his having earned it.

The Mercy Ball is a white sailcloth tent the size of a hangar, pitched on the south lawn between the House and the Italy, and inside it six hundred of the richest people between Fort Worth and El Paso are pretending to be at a barn dance. Outside, valets are parking Escalades in the hay stubble. An ice sculpture of the R-Bar-M brand, eight feet across, is melting from the M. Silver stock troughs of crushed ice and Mercy Ranch Water stand at every tent pole. The brisket flew in from Lockhart this afternoon on Mercy One along with its pitmaster, who is being photographed beside it like a groom.
This year’s theme is Boots & Bindings. The centerpieces are leather-bound classics, hollowed out and planted with succulents.
The Grapes of Wrath with a barrel cactus, which nobody on the committee found funny.

A Grammy-winning Western swing band from Austin plays “Faded Love” for people who have never faded at anything. On the forty-foot LED wall behind the stage, Colt — pearl snap open to the sternum, Stetson with a GoPro mount — is live to 2.1 million people. “We’re so back, Ranch Royalty,” Colt says, forty feet tall. “Shout-out to my cousin. Future king. Respectfully, bro.”

And down the middle of it all, led slowly between the tables so donors can stand beside him, comes a gray gelding named Deacon, who belongs to the Agriculture Commissioner and has his own handler and his own nondisclosure agreement.
“The horse tests at plus nine,” the Commissioner’s comms girl tells someone, not quietly enough.

Greer finds him in four seconds. She always does; he has a theory that she had him chipped, like a Labrador. Camel silk to the floor, a dark-blond blowout that has survived every wind West Texas has thrown at it, and the heirloom earrings she bought herself at an estate sale in River Oaks and lets people assume were her grandmother’s. She doesn’t ask where he was. Not yet. She takes his arm and talks into his shoulder at the volume of a woman saying something sweet.

“Agenda. One: Kilgore needs three minutes from you on rural water values. He doesn’t know what they are, so you’ll tell him. Two: Pete Ashworth bought a boat. Forty-eight feet. Say forty-eight like it’s a lot. Three: Soren Vale’s people want the heir in the photo line after the speech. That’s you. Smile like it’s you.” “Mm,” Whit says. “That’s mine,” she says. “Get your own.” Then she turns to face him, pulls loose his one-handed knot and ties his tie properly, fast and flat, in front of everyone: a half-Windsor with the dimple dead center. He loves her for it. Not simply, but really. It’s one of the things about her he would say under oath.

“Whit was always the gentle one,” his mother is telling Wes Kilgore and a Dallas donor in a bolo tie that cost more than the donor’s first house. “He’d cry over a coyote.” Chanel jacket over jeans, a cream cashmere wrap, enormous sunglasses pushed up into her silver chignon, and the cane she doesn’t need planted like a flag. Everybody laughs. Kilgore laughs a second too long and says, “Ma’am, I’m just a cowboy who took a wrong turn on the way to the rodeo and ended up in public service,” which has nothing to do with anything and which, Whit will learn, he says about every eleven minutes. Whit laughs too. It’s an old story. He has heard it every Christmas he can remember. Lorna kisses him on both cheeks, smelling of Shalimar and sparkling water, and tells him she is eleven years sober and drinking it all in.

His phone: a photo from Ximena. June at the window of her room in the Italy, nightgown and pink boots, nose flattened to the glass, waiting for fireworks that are almost two hours away. The caption reads: “She says she is on duty.” He sends back a shark, which in his family means I love you, and so does the shark.

A Patagonia vest over a tuxedo shirt and Luccheses so new they squeak: by the brisket, Soren Vale — founder of Halcyon Compute, guest of honor, the reason for the blue pipe on the stage — is explaining something to a rancher with both hands. The rancher has the expression of a man being told about his own cows.

Bunny Ashworth has a cluster of wives by the pecan pies, which flew in from Fredericksburg. She hums first — a bar of “Amazing Grace,” which with Bunny is the sound of a safety coming off — and then: “I’m not saying she’s a gold digger, sugar. I’m saying she brought her own shovel.” The wives make the sound of a flock settling. Whit follows their eyes across the tent, though he already knows where they’ll land.

Paloma is at the edge of the dance floor, alone, shoes back on as if they had never come off. Nobody is dancing near her. There’s a ring of empty parquet around her that is technically nobody’s fault. She’s turning the chip over her knuckles and watching the band like a dealer watching a table.

body.text: She doesn’t look at him. He’s grateful. He said something true in a church ten minutes ago and he can still feel it on him, like sun on the back of the neck, and he isn’t sure his face can be trusted with it yet.

He catches himself drafting it — the true thing he owes her — the way he drafts toasts: an opener, a turn, a button. Then he catches himself polishing the button, and stops, because he has a feeling she’d hear the polish from across the tent.
He keeps checking on her: the one person in the room he was rude to. She doesn’t look over. That’s fair. He keeps checking anyway.

body: At the far bar, under the string lights, his sister is talking low with Royce Teague. Hadley’s in a black tuxedo jumpsuit, a Patek on her wrist she would rather die than mention, her nails bitten to the quick. Teague is wearing aviators, at night, in a tent, and custom ostrich boots with his company’s ticker inlaid in turquoise up the shaft. He is not on the guest list. He is never on the guest list. He’s here anyway, the way a bill comes due. Teague laughs at something, big and white-veneered. Hadley doesn’t. Whit notes it and files it under Hadley being Hadley.

At 9:30 the band finishes a song and the lights over the head table come up, and his father’s chair is empty. It’s the tall chair, the only one at the table with arms. Amon Ransome has been on time for everything for seventy-six years, including, by family legend, his own birth. At cocktails he looked fine — six-four in a black tux and the silverbelly hat, receiving people by the ice brand like a bishop — though he kept his left hand in his pocket the whole hour, like a man guarding his wallet in Rome. Whit noticed the pocket. He decided it was a habit he’d never noticed. Greer looks at the chair, then at her watch. The band plays “Faded Love” again, louder.

At 9:31, across the tent, a phone lights Paloma’s face from below. He watches her read it. Her face changes — not much; a door closing somewhere in a big house — and it is the only time tonight he will see it do that in public. She puts the phone away. She leaves by the east flap, toward the barns, not hurrying, which is how Whit knows she’s hurrying.

choices.text: Follow her. Casually. You’re extremely casual.
choices.ledger: You left the tent four seconds after your father’s wife.
response: Somewhere behind him Bunny’s humming stops. He doesn’t hear it stop; he only notices, later, that it isn’t there anymore. He’s out the east flap before he has decided to be, walking with the specific nonchalance of a man who would like six hundred people to know he’s just getting some air.

choices.text: Text Greer — ‘Finding Dad’ — then go.
choices.ledger: You told Greer you were going to find your father.
response: He thumbs “Finding Dad” and is through the east flap before it delivers. Her reply lands in under three seconds: “Bring him in from the left. Cameras are right.” Then, a second bubble: “Thank you.” He stops in the dark grass to look at it. His wife almost never types that. She says it’s implied by the relationship.

choices.text: Ask Hadley where Dad is.
choices.ledger: You asked your sister for help. She gave it.
response: He cuts across the parquet to the far bar. Teague sees him coming and peels off with a clap on the shoulder — “Brother” — and a gust of cologne like a cigar humidor that has been to church. Hadley doesn’t watch him go.

“Where’s Dad?” “He was gray at cocktails.” She says it low, into her bourbon. “Don’t tell him I said gray.” And for a second there she is: the girl who pulled calves at three in the morning and never complained to anyone who could hear. “Go. I’ll stall Soren. I’ll explain groundwater law to him until he cries.”

s04.slug: EXT. BEHIND THE CUTTING BARN — NIGHT
body: The cutting barn shows the party its good side. Floodlights wash the front of it white; horse trailers stand in a row with their ramps down; a cutting exhibition ended twenty minutes ago and a few hands are still walking horses out, and warm air breathes from the open aisle, where the floor is radiant-heated so the horses won’t get cold feet. The floor cost forty thousand dollars. Hadley once worked it out at Thanksgiving, out loud, per horse, per winter.

Around back there is none of that. The light stops at the corner of the barn like a property line. Behind it: a caliche service road, white under the stars; a pipe fence; black pasture running off to nowhere; a windmill clanking somewhere out in the dark on a wind Whit can’t feel. From the tent, faint as a radio in somebody else’s car, Colt’s livestream: “—so back—”
He finds Paloma by the white of her arms.

body.text: She doesn’t look up. “You followed me.” “I followed—” He stops, because he’s seen what she’s kneeling beside. “Him.” “Okay.”

body: His father is on the ground. Amon Ransome, six-four, seventy-six, chairman and chief executive, is down on one hip on the caliche with his legs out in front of him like a child’s. His silverbelly hat lies upside down in the dirt a yard away. The black tuxedo is white with dust all down one side, the side he fell on. His left hand is out of his pocket now, and it’s shaking — not a tremble, not a cold man’s shiver, but a steady, mechanical shake, like something left running. Whit has never seen his father’s hand do anything it wasn’t told to do.

And Amon is talking. It’s the voice — the boardroom voice, deep and slow and Old Testament, the one that has fired company presidents and farriers with the same calm. “You’re on my land,” he says. “I told you. I told you once.” He’s looking past both of them, at the fence line. Whit looks at the fence line. There is nobody at the fence line. There’s the pipe fence and the dark and the windmill turning. He looks again, harder. Nobody.

Maybe it’s the dust. The chalky, burnt-lime smell of caliche coming up off his father’s coat, and his father on the ground, and the dark. Whit’s ribs go tight around nothing, and under the caliche there’s another smell he can’t place. Then it passes like a cramp, and he’s a grown man in a tuxedo behind a barn.
Stroke, he thinks, and the word is so big he can’t pick it up. “Okay,” he hears himself say. “Okay. Dad, we’re — we’re a little early for the after-party.” Nobody laughs. Not even him.

Paloma is on her knees on the caliche in her black dress with one palm flat on his father’s chest and the other holding his good hand, and she’s talking to him low and steady, the way you’d talk to a horse caught in wire. “Ya, ya. Tranquilo. Aquí estoy.” Then English, same voice: “It’s me. You’re at the Ball. You came out for some air. There’s nobody there.” She doesn’t look frightened. She doesn’t look surprised. She looks like someone doing a thing she has done before, and Whit notices that the way you notice a step that isn’t where it should be — and steps over it.

body.text: His phone buzzes in his pocket. Then again. Greer, wanting the left side of the tent. He doesn’t look.
Hadley said gray, he thinks. Hadley was right. Hadley is always right; it’s her worst quality, and he’d give a great deal right now for her to have been wrong once.

She looks up at him. “Whit.” It’s the first time she has ever said his name — not Mr. Ransome, not anything — and it reaches him even here, even now, with his father in the dirt, which he will think about later and not enjoy. “I need help,” she says. “Nobody else. Now.”
body.else: She looks up at him and tells him what she needs in short words, directions for someone who is already driving. “Help. Nobody else. Now.”

body: “Somebody films him inside ten minutes,” she says. “Three to one it’s Colt. It’s on Bunny’s Instagram by ten and on Bloomberg by Monday.” She isn’t being dramatic. She’s pricing it.
On the far side of the wall, the horses stand on their forty-thousand-dollar floor. On this side, the king sits on bare caliche, which nobody ever thought to heat.

Amon’s eyes come off the fence line and find his son. For two long seconds nothing happens in them. Whit watches his father look at him the way you look at a man in an airport who might be someone you went to school with. One. Two. Then it lands — Whit sees the exact moment it lands — and right behind recognition comes shame, enormous, and right behind shame, faster than anything, the old contempt, pulled over it like a tarp over a wreck. “Don’t stand there,” Amon says, “like a heifer at a gate.”

dossier.text: You found him on the ground behind the cutting barn during the Ball, ordering someone off his land. There was nobody there.

choices.text: Help her. Nobody sees.
choices.ledger: You and Paloma got your father inside without a soul seeing.
response: He gets down in the caliche — the knees of the tux go white at once — hooks his father’s hat out of the dirt with two fingers, and gets an arm under his father’s shoulder. Paloma takes the other side without being asked. Amon is heavier than any man should be, heavier than his size, as if he were made of something denser than other people.
“On three,” Paloma says, and counts in Spanish, and on tres they get him up. They go the dark way, through the back of the barn, where nobody is.

choices.text: Get Tack. Tack fixes things.
choices.ledger: You called Tack. He was already on his way.
response: His phone is out before he has finished deciding. Tack is the third favorite in it, after Greer and June’s school. It rings once. “I’m coming around the back, Bud.” Engine noise. Gravel. Tack is already driving.
Already. Whit hasn’t told him where. He looks at Paloma. She’s combing the caliche out of his father’s white hair with her fingers, and she doesn’t explain.

choices.text: Kneel. Say ‘Dad.’ Just that.
choices.ledger: You knelt in the caliche and called him Dad.
response: He kneels in the caliche, right in front of his father, close enough to smell the dust and the bourbon and the bay rum. He doesn’t say anything clever. He says the one word. “Dad.”

Amon’s eyes come to him from somewhere a long way off. Then his good hand closes on Whit’s wrist, hard, harder than a man of seventy-six should be able to grip anything, and he says, quite clearly, not to the man in front of him: “Get in the truck, son. Stay in the truck.”

Then he’s back. Whit watches him come back. And he is furious — furious to be seen, furious at the hand on the wrist, which he lets go of as if it belonged to somebody else. There is no truck. Whit doesn’t know why the sentence has made his hands go cold.
He picks up the hat. He gets an arm under his father’s shoulder, and Paloma takes the other side, and on her count they get him up.

s05.slug: INT. THE HOUSE — THE OLD ROOM — NIGHT
body: They go the dark way: through the back door of the cutting barn and down the long aisle, past stalls where horses swing their heads around to watch three people in evening clothes walk like one badly assembled animal. The floor is warm. Whit can feel it through his shoes, and he can feel his father feel it through his boots — a small, surprised give in the old man’s weight, as if he’d forgotten what money could do. Out the north end. Across forty yards of lawn the party lights don’t reach. Into the mudroom of the House: the old House, the 1928 limestone one, the one the Italy was later built around like a stucco fist.

The hall smells of saddle soap and Pledge, exactly as it did when he was six. Paloma steers. She knows which boards creak — the third one past the linen closet, the long one at the turn — and without a word she moves the three of them around both. Whit grew up in this house. He didn’t know about either board.

At the turn of the hall, framed in barnwood, hangs the Texas Monthly cover from 1986: his father at thirty-six on a fence rail, a buzzard on the post behind him, under the headline THE VULTURE OF MIDLAND. Amon hung it himself, at eye level. When people ask about it, he says it’s the nicest thing anyone wrote about him that decade.

The old room is at the end. Whit has been inside it maybe five times in his life, always summoned. It’s smaller than he remembers, which is the rule with rooms, but it’s more than that: it’s narrow, a cell, really, for a man who owns two hundred and twelve thousand acres. A narrow iron bed, made tight enough to bounce a quarter. A saddle on a wooden stand, oiled. A King James Bible on the nightstand with a rubber band around it, as if it might otherwise get out. A hat hook by the door. A 1970s Zenith radio in wood grain, its dial glowing faint orange, tuned to nothing.

And on the nightstand beside the Bible, a baby monitor. White plastic, one small green light. The same model as June’s. Whit knows it’s the same model because Greer had June’s overnighted from Dallas after reading forty reviews aloud to him in bed. He looks at it. He decides not to think about it. He has been told he’s extremely good at that.

Paloma gets Amon onto the edge of the bed. She opens his collar, two studs, and drops them in her palm without looking. She runs water in the little bathroom and brings it back in a glass and holds it until his good hand takes it. She takes the hat from Whit — he didn’t know he was still holding it — and hangs it on the hook. All of it fast, unshowy, in order, like a pit crew.

And Amon puts himself back together in front of them. Whit watches it happen. It takes about four minutes. First the breathing slows. Then the shoulders come back. The left hand goes into the pocket of the tux and stays there. The eyes, which were somewhere else, come home and clear and narrow, and the face that has frightened three generations of Texas oilmen reassembles itself piece by piece, like a man buckling on armor in a hurry and getting every buckle. In four minutes he is nearly the lion again. Nearly. There’s still dust in his hair.

body.text: He won’t look at Whit at all. Not once, not even by accident. He looks at the saddle, the radio, the glass in his hand, the black window, anywhere else. Whit stands by the door with his arms at his sides and can still feel the grip on his wrist, a bracelet of pressure, as if his father had left something there and gone.

When he speaks, he says it to the window. “A man who needs to be liked,” Amon says, coldly and clearly, “will be owned by whoever likes him.” Whit has known his father for thirty-three years and can translate. It means thank you. It also means get out.

It means thank you. It also means get out.

body: Paloma walks him out. In the hall she pulls the door almost shut behind her — not all the way; she leaves a hand’s width, and Whit sees her glance once at the gap, measuring it — and they stand in the narrow hall under the Vulture of Midland, close, because the hall was built in 1928 for thinner people with less to say to each other.

Up close she smells of cedar and caliche. They both do. There is pale dust on the black of her dress and pale dust on his lapel, and she reaches up and brushes his lapel with two flat strokes of her hand, quick and practical, a saddle-brushing stroke — and then stops, her hand still raised, as if she has caught herself doing something in public. She puts the hand down.

body.text: “You said you were afraid he’d pick you,” she says. “You should see your face right now.” “What’s my face doing?” “It’s afraid he won’t.”

body: “Nobody,” she says, very quietly, because the door is open a hand’s width. “Not your wife. Not your sister. Nobody.” “Paloma—” “Not for me. For him.” She tips her head at the door. “He’s going to walk out there in fifteen minutes and stand up in front of six hundred people, and he needs this to have never happened. Can you give him that?”

choices.text: Promise. Mean it.
choices.ledger: You promised Paloma you’d tell no one about the barn.
response: “I promise,” he says. No joke on it. He finds he means it all the way down, which is not a place he goes often.
She looks at him until it becomes a little uncomfortable, then very uncomfortable, then something else. She checks his math. “Okay,” she says.
She believes him. He watches her decide to. And walking back out through the mudroom toward the noise, he finds he very much wants to be the kind of man who deserves it.

choices.text: ‘Scout’s honor.’ You were never a Scout.
choices.ledger: You promised Paloma, sort of. Scout’s honor.
response: He holds up three fingers. “Scout’s honor.” “You weren’t a Scout.” “I was asked to leave the Scouts.” “Why?” “Charm.”
Her face nearly laughs, and swallows it before it reaches the hall. “Okay,” she says. “I’ll take sort of.”

choices.text: Ask her what’s wrong with him.
choices.ledger: You asked Paloma what’s wrong with your father. She didn’t answer.
response: “What’s wrong with him?” “He fell.” “That’s not an answer.” “It’s the one he’d give.”

She waits. The hall waits with her. He doesn’t promise. He stands there in the dust and doesn’t, and he watches her notice that he doesn’t — and, oddly, she seems to think better of him for it, not worse.
“Go be charming,” she says. “Fifteen minutes.”

s05b.slug: EXT./INT. TACK’S SILVERADO — THE BARN ROAD — NIGHT
body: Tack comes up the caliche with his headlights off. Whit hears the truck before he sees it — the particular ruined purr of a 2004 Silverado with six hundred thousand miles on it, which Tack won’t replace because “a new one asks questions” — and then it’s there, a darker shape on the white road, rolling the last thirty feet in neutral so it barely makes a sound.

Tack gets out. Sixty-seven, small and leathery, white mustache, reading glasses on a string around his neck. He’s wearing a pearl-snap shirt buttoned to the throat under a tuxedo jacket that doesn’t fit him across the shoulders. The jacket is rented. Odell Tackett has run a ranch that grew a twelve-car garage and a chandelier in it for thirty-five years, and he has never owned a tuxedo, and he never will. Every October he rents one from a place in Midland and returns it Monday with the receipt.

He doesn’t ask what happened. He crouches by Amon, says “All right, now” to nobody in particular, gets a shoulder under him and lifts — a man nearly a foot taller and fifty pounds heavier — into the cab of the truck in one smooth, unhurried motion, like a bale he’s loaded a thousand of. You don’t get a motion like that the first time. You get it by doing it before.

Tack and Paloma talk across Amon in short words, low, like two people who have worked the same night shift for months and quit using whole sentences. “I’ve got him, Mrs. Ransome.” “His collar.” “I know.” Tack opens the old man’s collar with two fingers. On the dash a Thermos of Folgers rolls when the door shuts and comes to rest against the windshield.

body.text: Tack looks at Whit. Then at Paloma. Then back at Whit, over the glasses, for a while. “Well,” he says. That’s all.

body: Then he turns to Whit, mild as milk. “Go on back to your party, Bud. Your daddy took a turn on the gravel. That’s all this was.”
It’s a perfect sentence. No edges. It sounds like a press release that’s been waiting for the right night.

Paloma climbs into the cab beside his father and pulls the door to. Through the open window she holds out her hand, and Whit realizes he’s holding his father’s hat. He must have picked it up out of the dirt; he doesn’t remember doing it. The engine idles. The windmill clanks. Tack puts the truck in gear and keeps his boot on the brake, waiting, the way he has always waited for Whit — patient as a fence post — to finish doing whatever Whit is going to do.

dossier.text: Drives a 2004 Silverado with 600,000 miles because ‘a new one asks questions.’ Was already on his way to the barn when you called.

choices.text: Go back. Tack’s got it. Tack’s always got it.
choices.ledger: You let Tack handle it. He said that’s all it was.
response: He hands the hat through the window. Paloma sets it on her knees, crown down, the way you’re supposed to.
“Good man,” Tack says, and lifts two fingers off the wheel, and the truck rolls off with its lights still out. Whit stands behind the barn hating how good that felt.

choices.text: Climb in the bed of the truck. In the tux.
choices.ledger: You rode to the House in the bed of Tack’s truck, in your tuxedo.
response: He doesn’t hand over the hat. He puts a hand on the tailgate and goes over it into the bed of the truck, in the tux, and lands on a coil of baling wire and a sack of mineral lick. Tack looks at him in the rearview mirror for a long moment. Then he lets off the brake.

Two hundred yards of caliche at five miles an hour: Whit on his knees in the truck bed, holding the rail with one hand and his father’s hat with the other, the dust coming up white around him as if he’s being sifted.

At the House, Tack and Paloma get Amon out between them, and Paloma lets Whit carry the hat in through the mudroom and down the hall, past the Texas Monthly cover from 1986 — his father at thirty-six on a fence rail, under THE VULTURE OF MIDLAND — as far as the door at the end, and no further. There she takes the hat out of his hands.
“Fifteen minutes,” she says. “Go be charming.” The door closes, gently, on his face.

choices.text: Ask Tack how many times he’s done this.
choices.cue: Tack said nothing. He usually doesn’t.
choices.ledger: You asked Tack how many times he’s done this.
response: He hands the hat through the window. Then, before he can talk himself out of it: “Tack. How many times have you done this?”
Tack looks at him over the reading glasses. It is a long look, perfectly friendly, the look of a man who has outwaited droughts. “Done what, Bud?”
Whit doesn’t have a word for what. Tack waits to see whether he’ll find one. He doesn’t. “Well,” says Tack, and lets off the brake.

As the truck slides past, Paloma looks at Whit through the open window — one look, quick — and he reads it as good question. He may be wrong. Then the truck is gone up the road, and he’s alone with the windmill.

s06.slug: EXT. THE MERCY BALL TENT — NIGHT
body: 9:54. Whit comes back in through the west flap with the night still on him. The band is into “San Antonio Rose,” the fiddle doing the work the singer can’t, and three hundred couples who between them own a respectable fraction of the Permian Basin are two-stepping on a floor rented from a company in Dripping Springs. On the forty-foot wall, Colt is interviewing Deacon. “Deacon, real talk. How are we feeling about the Senate?” Deacon is feeling nothing about the Senate. Deacon is eating a succulent out of a hollowed-out Moby-Dick, and the stream’s comment count is climbing the side of the screen like a fever.

He looks down. There’s caliche on his trouser cuffs: the pale chalk dust of West Texas, the stuff they spread on lease roads by the ton, the stuff that gets into everything and stays. He bends and brushes at it. It smears. He brushes again and makes it worse, a man in a six-thousand-dollar Tom Ford tuxedo slapping at his own ankles beside the dessert table, and he straightens up before anybody can decide it means something.

body.text: Across the tent the service door opens and Tack comes in from the north, tugging straight a rented tux jacket that was cut for a larger and more confident man. He takes up his post beside the door — same post, same angle, hands folded over his belt buckle — as if he’d never left it. Nobody looks at him. Nobody has looked at Tack at a party in thirty years. It occurs to Whit, for the first time in his life, to wonder whether that’s on purpose.

Over by the brisket station Hadley has Soren Vale backed against a carving board and is talking with both hands: acre-feet, drawdown, the drought of the fifties, the Rule of Capture as a concept and as a weapon. Soren nods like a man being shown photographs of a surgery he didn’t consent to. Over Soren’s shoulder Hadley finds Whit and taps the face of the Patek twice. Nine minutes, Golden. You owe me nine minutes.

body: Greer is at his elbow before he’s finished straightening. She doesn’t say anything. She takes a linen napkin off the nearest table — Table Nine, the Ashworths, a hollowed-out Lonesome Dove sprouting an aloe — and kneels. Kneels, in camel silk, on a rented dance floor, in front of six hundred people, and goes at his cuffs herself in short hard strokes, like buffing a boot.

She talks up at him with a smile aimed at the room. Anyone watching sees a wife fussing over her husband, which is the most flattering thing a Fort Worth wife can be seen doing in public. Bunny Ashworth, two tables over, watches, and for once doesn’t hum.

body.text: “Did you find him?” is the first thing she says, low, under the fiddle, and it’s a real question; for a second she sounds like a person and not a firm. He nods. She nods. She held up her end tonight, he told her where he was going, and so what comes next comes gentler than he deserves. “You were gone twenty-three minutes, Whit.” Stroke. Stroke. “So was she.”
body.else: “You were gone twenty-three minutes,” she says pleasantly, to his shins. Stroke. Stroke. “So was she.”

body.text: “Bunny says you left four seconds after her.” Stroke. “Bunny counts.”

body: She folds the napkin over the dirt so the dirt doesn’t show and keeps working. “I don’t care where you put it, Whitaker.” Stroke. “I care who sees you carry it.”

He heard her say it once before, about a different thing. It frightens him now exactly as it did then. Under the fright is a comfort he’s ashamed of: a woman who will kneel on a dance floor so no one sees him dirty.

She stands. A knee pops; she doesn’t acknowledge it. Behind her a donor in a bolo tie is explaining the ice sculpture to one of Soren’s vice presidents, who is wearing Soren’s exact vest in a smaller size. “Guy from the Ice Hotel in Sweden. Flew him in. He said our heat was a creative challenge.” The R-Bar-M behind them is down to an R, a bar, and a suggestion.

Greer’s reading glasses come out of her clutch, folded, and she holds them by the hinge like a gavel she hasn’t decided to bring down. “Item one,” she says. She lets the band finish a phrase. “Where were you.”
She waits. The fiddle waits. Up on the forty-foot wall, Deacon has found a second book.

choices.text: Tell her. Dad fell behind the barn.
choices.ledger: You told Greer your father fell behind the cutting barn.
response: So he tells her. He does it quietly and out of order, the way true things come out of him: the hat in the dirt, the tux gone white with dust, the left hand going like a struck wire. Then the part he hadn’t planned on saying. “He was talking to somebody, Greer. Out at the fence. Telling him to get off the land.” He hears his own voice drop. “There was nobody there.”
Greer’s glasses go on and come straight back off. “Which fence.” “The pipe fence. Out back, toward the windmill.” She looks at him for exactly as long as it takes to file it.

“Mm.” Then the firm comes back online, all at once, like the lights after a storm. “Take me to him. Now.” She’s already moving, already smiling at Pete Ashworth as they pass his table. “If he’s down, I need to see it with my own eyes before Hadley does.”

choices.text: Tell her. You promised Paloma — tell her anyway.
choices.ledger: You told Greer about the barn. You’d promised Paloma you wouldn’t.
response: So he tells her, quietly and out of order: the hat in the dirt, the tux gone white, the left hand going like a struck wire. Then the part he hadn’t planned on saying. “He was talking to somebody, Greer. Out at the fence. There was nobody there.” Greer’s glasses go on and come straight back off. “Which fence.”
The promise is not five minutes old. He can hear exactly how long it lasted. It lasted less than one fiddle break.

“Mm.” Then the firm comes back online, all at once. “Take me to him. Now.” She’s already moving, already smiling at Pete Ashworth as they pass. “If he’s down, I need to see it with my own eyes before Hadley does.”

choices.text: ‘The powder room in the Italy. The gold swan one.’
choices.ledger: You told Greer you were in the gold swan powder room.
response: “Powder room in the Italy,” he says. “The gold swan one. We needed a minute alone with the swan.”

“The swan’s been roped off since four,” Greer says. “Pete Ashworth’s nephew was sick in it. There’s a man from ServiceMaster in there right now with an industrial fan.” She lets that sit. She lets it sit long enough for him to hear the fan.

“Mm.” And then she takes his hand and squeezes it, a real squeeze, warm and dry and brief, and walks him toward the head table smiling at everyone they pass, as if the lie were a present he’d brought her and she has decided to keep it. For later.

choices.text: Tell her about the chapel. Leave out the barn.
choices.ledger: You told Greer you were in the chapel. You didn’t mention the barn.
response: “Rehearsing,” he says. “In the chapel.”
“In the chapel.”
“It has great acoustics.”

Greer doesn’t answer. She turns her phone around. It’s already open — of course it’s already open — to @cuervocountycouture, the anonymous account that everybody from Midland to Highland Park knows is Bunny. Posted 9:15: Paloma on the chapel path in the dark, barefoot, black dress, her shoes hanging from two fingers. Caption: “Somebody’s been to church 🙏🕊️.” Two thousand likes. One of them is Colt. “Mm,” says Greer, and puts the phone away. “Smile. You’re on the wall.”

s06b.slug: INT. THE HOUSE — THE OLD HALL — NIGHT
body: 9:58. Greer crosses the south lawn in four-inch heels at a speed that would get a horse disqualified. “We have eight minutes,” she says, without looking at her watch, because she is the watch. The grass is wet. It’s the only green lawn in Cuervo County in October, watered every night out of the aquifer the company is about to sell, and it’s soaking the hem of her dress, and she doesn’t slow down.

The House takes them in by the mudroom door, out of the noise. Saddle soap and Pledge, seventy years of boots on the same pine. On the hall wall, the framed 1986 Texas Monthly cover: his father at thirty-six on a fence rail with a buzzard on the post behind him, grinning, THE VULTURE OF MIDLAND, still at eye level. The caption says he bought half of Midland for pennies the year everybody else went broke. Three separate publicists have asked him to take it down. Two of them no longer work in Texas.

Greer passes it without a glance. At the old room door she stops, squares her shoulders and knocks: three knocks, evenly spaced, the knock you use on a deposition room when you already know what’s inside.

body.text: Tack is already in the hall. He must have seen them leave the tent and come by the service path, which is shorter and which nobody but Tack uses; he’s standing beside the door like a piece of furniture that came with the House, hat in his hands, breathing no harder than the furniture. “Evening, Miss Greer.” “Odell.” She’s the only person alive who calls him that. Greer knows it, Tack knows she knows it, and Whit, standing between them, has the feeling of watching two contractors nod at each other across a job site he doesn’t have a hard hat for.

body: The door opens four inches. Paloma. Shoes back on — the invoices — dress smoothed, not a grain of the barn on her anywhere. “Paloma,” Greer says warmly. “Greer,” Paloma says, exactly as warm, and they trade each other’s names like people passing a hot pan, neither letting on.
“I’d like to see Amon.”
“He’s resting.”
“I’m family,” Greer says.
“So am I,” says Paloma. “That’s the joke everyone tells.”

Neither of them raises her voice. Neither of them would. Greer makes her case the way she’d make it to a board: she runs the family office; in eight minutes the chairman is due on a stage in front of six hundred people, a United States Senate candidate, a horse, and a man from California with a three-billion-dollar check; she needs to know, for planning purposes, whether he can stand. “For planning purposes,” Greer repeats, kindly, as if Paloma might not have the vocabulary.
“He can stand,” Paloma says. “He’s standing.”
From inside the room, through four inches of door, comes the voice: the lion, or a very good recording of one. “Who’s out there?”
Nobody answers him. Paloma’s eyes go to Whit and stay there for one second. It’s all over his face; it always has been.

body.text: The look isn’t angry. He could survive angry; he grew up in a house built out of it. It’s the look of someone redoing a sum she thought she had right: carrying a number, crossing something out, arriving at a new figure for what he’s worth.
And it lands on Whit, standing in the hall he grew up in, that his wife is about to get in one minute the answer he couldn’t get in five. He asked. Greer doesn’t ask. Greer knocks.

body: Greer’s phone buzzes. She answers it with one thumb, never looking down, her eyes on Paloma the whole time. Whit reads it upside down, a skill seven years of marriage have given him: Kilgore’s campaign manager, all caps, asking where they want Deacon for the speech. Greer types, “Horse out of the tent before the speech. Plus nine is not plus nine if it shits.” Send. She touches one of the earrings and goes on looking at Paloma as if the text never happened.
Three people in a narrow hall, and behind a door a fourth, who used to fill any room he walked into and is now being argued over like a parking space.

choices.text: Stand with Greer. ‘She’s my wife, Paloma.’
choices.ledger: You stood with your wife at your father’s door.
response: “She’s my wife, Paloma.” It comes out gentler than he means and firmer than he expected. Paloma looks at him a moment longer. Then she opens the door all the way.

Amon is upright in the leather chair beside the Zenith, collar closed, tie retied, the hat back on his head. Magnificent, and the color of ash. He looks straight past his son to Greer and says, “Satisfied, Mrs. Ransome?” The name hangs in the doorway, because there are two Mrs. Ransomes in it and he hasn’t said which.

Greer is satisfied. She is also, Whit sees, looking at his father’s left hand, which is on the arm of the chair and shaking, until Amon notices her noticing and puts it in his pocket. Whit sees her see it. Paloma sees Whit see it. Out on the lawn, the band starts the next song.

choices.text: Stand with Paloma. ‘He said nobody, Greer.’
choices.ledger: You took Paloma’s side against your wife.
response: “He said nobody, Greer.”

It isn’t quite true. It was Paloma who said nobody, behind the barn, on her knees in the dirt. The second it’s out of his mouth he can hear that everyone in the hall knows exactly whose word he’s keeping.
Paloma doesn’t thank him. She closes the door gently, and the latch clicks.

Greer turns to him with the face she wore at the refinery-fire press conference, the face that got two dead men described on the evening news as a tragic exception to an exemplary safety record: composed, sympathetic, unreadable. “Mm.” On the lawn she takes his arm as if nothing has happened.

choices.text: Make it a joke and herd everybody back to the party.
choices.ledger: You made a joke at your father’s door and herded everyone back to the Ball.
response: “Ladies.” He spreads his arms, one hand toward each of them, a man herding cattle that outrank him. “Respectfully, and I mean that with love and genuine terror, the man has a speech. Let’s let him put his face on.”

From inside, the lion bellows and ends it for all of them. “Get out. All of you. I’ll be there when I’m there.” It rattles the Zenith on its shelf. It’s a good voice. It’s the voice that bought half of Midland in 1986.

Paloma closes the door. Greer has heard him; she hasn’t seen a thing. She takes Whit’s arm on the way out, and he can feel her deciding the voice will do for now, the way you sign for a package you mean to open later, alone, with a knife.

s07.slug: EXT. THE MERCY BALL TENT — THE STAGE — NIGHT
body: 10:06. The lights drop. The band stops in the middle of a bar, which the band has been paid not to mind. A spotlight finds the stage steps, and Amon Ransome walks up them.

No stiff steps. No hand. No dust. Whit has to look twice to believe it, then a third time, because he can’t find the seam. His father crosses the stage in a clean black tux and the silverbelly Open Road he has worn since 1974 — eleven hats, one hat — with the long, unbothered stride of a man who has never in his life been on the ground behind anything, and the tent rises for him. Six hundred people who paid twenty-five thousand dollars a table to be here stand up like a congregation. Whit stands with them. His knees decide before he does.

At the side of the stage, in the dark just past the edge of the light, Paloma stands with her hands folded in front of her. She isn’t watching the crowd and she isn’t watching his face. She’s watching his feet. Tack is at the service door. Lorna is at Table Two in her wrap, applauding with two fingers against her palm: museum applause. Bunny has her phone up.

body.text: Whit watches the left hand. It goes into the trouser pocket at the top of the steps and stays there, and it will stay there for the whole speech. Having carried the man, Whit knows what that costs. He has never been so proud of his father, or so afraid of him.

Whit thinks: half an hour ago he was in the dirt. And Tack said that’s all it was, a turn on the gravel, and now look at him. Maybe that is all it was. Whit would very much like that to be all it was. Standing, applauding, he decides that it was.
Beside him, Greer isn’t watching the speech. She’s watching his father’s left hand — the pocket, the shape of the fist inside it — with the calm professional attention of someone counting the exits.

Greer doesn’t touch him. She always touches him during speeches: a hand on his sleeve, a knuckle at the small of his back, small corrections, a jockey’s hands. Tonight she sits a careful inch away and applauds exactly as much as everyone else.
Greer’s hand finds his knee under the tablecloth, light and proprietary, the way you’d rest a hand on the hood of a car you’ve already paid off.
Across the family table Hadley catches his eye and lifts her bourbon a quarter of an inch. You’re welcome.

body: “Sit down,” Amon says into the microphone, and they do, and he lets them sit in the quiet longer than is comfortable. Whit has watched his father use silence his whole life: at closings, at Whit’s eighth-grade parent-teacher conference, which the vice principal ended early, in tears. Nobody in the tent can tell what the pauses are for. That has always been the trick of them.

“In 1923,” Amon says, “my grandfather put a bit into this ground a mile from where you’re sitting, and the ground gave him back oil. One month after Santa Rita. He never forgave the University of Texas for beating him by a month.” Warm laughter; the UT regent at Table Six laughs loudest. “He thanked God and kept drilling. That is the whole of the Ransome theology. Thank God and keep drilling.” The pause. “A hundred and three years. When oil went to ten dollars in 1986, we were cattle. When the cattle went to hell in the drought of 2011, we were oil. We have been whatever this state needed, and we have charged it fair.” The pause. “Mostly fair.”

Bigger laughter. Behind him the LED wall dissolves to the line Ransome Horizon paid an agency in Austin four hundred thousand dollars to write, ENERGY FOR THE NEXT TEXAS, over drone footage of a pronghorn that, Whit happens to know, was rented.

Then Amon leans on the podium and looks down at the board table — eleven directors, eleven spouses, a retired ExxonMobil executive asleep with his eyes open — and says, mildly, “I have buried better men than this board.”

The tent roars. Pete Ashworth roars loudest and slaps the table. Whit laughs too. It’s a great line; it has been a great line at every Ransome function since Whit was in diapers, and his father’s timing on it is, as always, perfect.

“Now.” The laughter thins. “Everybody in this tent came out here tonight to see me name my heir.” He lets it hang. Whit can feel the two index cards in his breast pocket, the third one still face down on a pew six hundred yards west. Greer’s hand, wherever it is, stops.
“I’m not going to.”
Silence. Then the laugh a crowd gives when it hopes it’s being joked with. It isn’t. Amon waits for the laugh to die, and lets it die all the way.

“I have run cattle for sixty years,” he says. “You don’t buy a yearling for its papers. You put it in the pen and you turn out a cow, and you watch what it does. Does it read the cow. Does it hold. Does it quit.” The pause. “I have two children. I am going to put them in the pen.”

“For one year, starting Monday, Hadley” — the name in full, struck like a gavel — “and my son” — two words that land on Whit like a demotion with a bow on it — “will each carry the weight of this company. A real piece of it. A piece that can kill them. And at the end of that year I will name the one who earned it, and the other one can go to work for them. Or go to Dallas.” A huge laugh; Dallas always gets a laugh. “Assignments Monday. Fort Worth. Eight a.m. Wear boots you can walk in.”

The 9:40 slot dies quietly in Whit’s breast pocket: Greer’s bullet points, the Cowboys joke, one self-deprecating line and no more than one. All of it cancelled by a man who never checked with the program.

Across the table, Hadley is thirty-seven years old. She has carried the weight of this company since she was twenty-four, including the April afternoon in 2020 when oil went to minus thirty-seven dollars a barrel and she ran the whole Permian from the cab of a pickup on a lease road with two phones and a legal pad. She has just been told, in front of six hundred people, that all of it was practice.

Before anyone can decide what to do with their face, Amon raises his good hand and says, “Now for the good news,” and Soren Vale comes up the steps. Patagonia vest over a tuxedo shirt. Lucchese boots so new they squeak on the stage; the podium mic catches every step, like a dog toy. He shakes Amon’s hand with both of his, the way men from California shake hands with men they’ve read about.

Project Wellspring. Amon says it like scripture and Soren says it like a launch. Whit knew the number — Greer briefed him in August, in bed, under NDA — but not the pipe, not the pastor, not that it would be tonight. Twenty years. Three point one billion dollars. Gas-fired power from Ransome wells, and nine million gallons a day of West Texas groundwater from under the Mercy, piped up the road to Halcyon Compute’s two-gigawatt Lariat Campus, where, Soren explains, glowing, the future will be trained. “We don’t build data centers,” Soren says. “We build the place where Texas teaches the future to think.” Somebody at Table Fourteen says amen. Soren says, “Exactly.” The wall goes a hopeful blue: THE WELLSPRING COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIP, in a typeface that has been to Austin. Four hundred jobs for Pardee. A new imaging wing for Ransome Memorial. Scholarships. A splash pad.

Then Pastor Jimmy Don Quick of Lone Star Cathedral, Midland — eleven thousand members and a satellite campus in a former Bass Pro Shop — comes up in a dove-gray suit, and two men from Ransome Midstream carry out a three-foot length of blue pipe tied with a white satin bow. The pastor lays both hands on it and closes his eyes. “Lord,” he says, reading the last word off an index card from Halcyon’s communications team, “bless this pipe, and the water that will flow through it, and the inference it will make possible.” He doesn’t know what inference is. He blesses it anyway. Six hundred people bow their heads to a pipe.

body.text: During the applause it comes back to him, unasked: Stay in the truck. His father’s grip on his wrist, his father’s voice from somewhere far off. Then the band hits a sting and it’s gone, like a word you reach for.

body: Whit is still applauding when he notices the room has stopped looking at the stage.

Colt has found him. Of course Colt has found him. Colt has been finding people at their worst since he got his first GoPro at twelve, and Colt loves him, which doesn’t help. The forty-foot wall cuts from the blessed pipe to the family table, and there’s Whit’s face, ten feet high and in perfect focus, at the exact moment his father finishes not choosing him. In the corner of the screen, little hearts float up. 41.2K WATCHING. Six hundred people turn from the stage to the screen to see how he takes it.
He can see himself seeing himself.

choices.text: Make it a joke. Raise your glass: ‘To the Trial. I’ve always tested well.’
choices.ledger: Your father passed you over on a forty-foot screen. You got the biggest laugh of the night.
response: He picks up his glass. He finds Colt’s lens like an old friend at a reunion. He raises the glass to the forty-foot version of himself and says, loud enough for the table mics, “To the Trial.” He lets a pause go by, his father’s trick. He learned it somewhere. “I’ve always tested well.”

The tent comes apart. It’s the biggest laugh of the night, bigger than buried better men. The two board independents laugh hardest, the ones who go wherever the stock goes, and Whit watches them decide he’s a good sport, which on this board is a kind of currency. Pete Ashworth slaps the table again. Bunny stops humming to laugh.
Amon, at the podium, doesn’t laugh. Across the table, Hadley’s glass comes down very, very slowly, until it touches the cloth without a sound.

choices.text: Stand. Applaud him. Mean some of it.
choices.ledger: You stood and applauded your father for passing you over.
response: He stands. He doesn’t decide to; he’s simply up, chair pushed back, hands coming together, and for a long second he’s the only person on his feet in a tent of six hundred, applauding the man who has just declined to choose him.

Then the room follows him up. Table by table: the board, the Ashworths, the Midland money and the Dallas money, Kilgore with his hat over his heart for some reason, until the whole tent is standing because the son stood. On the wall his face is clear and warm and very nearly true. He means about half of it. He’s surprised it’s that much.

Amon finds him in the light from the podium. Holds there. Then nods once, a short dip of the hat brim: the nod Whit has seen him give a horse that worked, and, until tonight, not once to anybody he’s related to.

choices.text: Smile. Leave.
choices.ledger: You smiled for the camera and walked out of your father’s speech.
response: He smiles at the camera. It’s a great smile, the one from the Ransome Christmas card, the one with the Bible and the rifle and the Labrador, styled by a woman from Los Angeles who called him “a really giving face.” Ten feet high, it doesn’t flicker.

Then he stands, buttons his jacket — one button, the way his mother taught him — and walks out. Not fast. Down the side aisle, past the Ashworths, past the ice brand weeping into its tray, past Tack at the service door, who doesn’t move, and out the west flap into the dark.

Colt’s camera follows him to the edge of the light and loses him there. For three seconds the forty-foot wall shows nothing but a canvas flap swinging. Then it cuts back to the tent, and on the screen six hundred people are watching him go.

s08.slug: EXT. THE MERCY BALL — THE FAR BAR — NIGHT
body: 10:30. The far bar sits at the very edge of things, where the sailcloth gives out and the string lights carry on alone over the grass, as if they’ve been told the party continues and are too polite to check. It’s the bar for people who want to be found only by people who are looking. The bartender, a man bun from Austin with a Railroad Commission seal tattooed on his forearm that he got, he tells everyone, ironically, is building a forty-dollar Ranch Water: Lalo, lime, Topo Chico, and then, because the events manager is watching, a ceremonial splash of Mercy Ranch Water from the can, so it can go on the card as estate.

Taped inside the bar where only the bartender can see it is a typed list headed KILGORE — DO NOT SERVE ON CAMERA. Tito’s. Gin. Topo Chico. Water. Anything clear. Underneath, in Sharpie, in the comms girl’s round hand: “Clear reads as vodka. Vodka reads as Austin.”

Royce Teague is leaving as Whit arrives, which feels arranged and probably was. He’s in a white dinner jacket nobody has worn sincerely since 1962, with a pistol-grip belt buckle and aviators on at half past ten at night. He claps Whit on the shoulder hard enough to count as a contact sport. “Brother.” Whit has never been his brother. “The Lord made oil and the Lord made lawyers, and I thank Him for both.” He winks at Hadley over Whit’s shoulder. Then he walks out from under the string lights into the black pasture like a man with a deed to the dark.

Hadley stays where she is. Black tux jumpsuit, a bourbon neat she isn’t drinking so much as consulting. She has bitten the nail of her right index finger down to the pink and started on the next one. She doesn’t look at Whit when he leans on the bar beside her. She looks at the bright heart of the tent, where their father is shaking hands with a line of people that runs out the flap.

body.text: “‘I’ve always tested well,’” Hadley says. “That was good, Golden. Really. You tested well at Deerfield, too. They gave you a scar and a diploma.” She isn’t laughing. He tries to remember the last time he saw her laugh at something he said and gets as far as the Clinton administration.

“Nice standing ovation.” She turns her glass a quarter-turn on the bar. “You started it. You know that, right? Dad saw who started it.” It sounds like an accusation, and then, about halfway through, it doesn’t. “It was the right thing. I hate that you did the right thing. I’d have done it if I’d thought of it. I didn’t think of it, because I was busy wanting to set the tent on fire.”

“I bought you nine minutes with Soren,” she says. “Nine minutes of acre-feet. He asked me whether aquifers were renewable, and I watched him find out. You spent those nine minutes somewhere.” She waits. “Where?” Whit doesn’t answer. Hadley doesn’t push. When Hadley doesn’t push, she’s writing something down.

Whit wonders whether Greer has already told her. Greer has had half an hour, and Greer can do a great deal with half an hour. He looks at his sister’s face for the answer and gets nothing. With Hadley, he never can.

body: “I’ve run the numbers on your charm, Golden,” she says at last. “It depreciates. Straight-line. You’ve got maybe six years left on it, and then you’re just a tall man at a party.” She drinks, finally. “And you want to know the actual joke? He’s not picking a successor, Golden. He’s picking a witness.”
Hadley’s fury, for once, isn’t aimed at him.
Colt drifts by under the string lights, phone on a gimbal, narrating. “Okay, okay, okay, the siblings, at the bar, post-Trial, the vibes are immaculate, we are so back —”
“Colt,” Hadley says, without turning her head. “Off.”
Colt goes off. He goes off so fast he walks into a hay bale, and then apologizes to the hay bale, on camera, because he’s Colt.

Then, out of nowhere, in the voice she’d use to read a production report: “I was twelve. Junior cutting championship, Will Rogers. I’d been on that horse at five every morning for a year. Little sorrel mare named Dolly Parton.” A sip. “I marked a seventy-four. Highest junior score in the state that year. Dad wasn’t there. Dad was here, watching you fall off a pony.” She says it like a stat, like an EBITDA figure. “You were eight. The pony was called Peanut. He sat with you at Ransome Memorial all afternoon. It was a sprained wrist.”
Whit doesn’t remember the pony. He doesn’t remember the wrist. She remembers the pony’s name.
Hadley finishes the nail.

choices.text: Ask her what Teague wanted.
choices.ledger: You asked Hadley what Royce Teague wanted.
response: “What did Royce Teague want?” He says it lightly. It doesn’t land lightly. Hadley turns and looks at him, really looks, for the first time since he came to the bar.

“To be invited,” she says. Smooth. Too smooth. Hadley is never smooth, Hadley is sandpaper, and the smoothness is the only thing in the answer he’s sure of. She finishes the bourbon in one swallow and sets the glass down with a click.
“He’s a clown with a podcast, Golden. Barrels and Bibles. Last week he had a man on who thinks the Permian is God’s apology for Oklahoma.” She pushes off the bar. “Worry about Monday.”

choices.text: Tell her Dad fell.
choices.ledger: You told Hadley your father fell behind the barn.
response: “Hads.” He keeps his voice down. “Dad fell. Behind the cutting barn, before the speech. He was on the ground. For a second he didn’t know who I was.”
She goes white under the sunburn. It starts at her collar and climbs, and for one second she’s thirteen. “Gray,” she says. “He was gray at cocktails. I said gray.”

Then she’s the COO again. He watches it happen: the shoulders coming down, the eyes sliding a little to the left, where she keeps her spreadsheets. He watches her decide what this is worth — to the board, to Monday, to the year. “Thank you,” she says. “I mean that.” She does. That’s the problem.

choices.text: Tell her Dad fell.
choices.ledger: You told Hadley your father fell behind the barn.
response: “Hads.” He keeps his voice down. “Dad fell. Behind the cutting barn, before the speech. He was on the ground. For a second he didn’t know who I was.”
She goes white under the sunburn. It starts at her collar and climbs. “Gray,” she says, to herself. “He was gray at cocktails. I thought, don’t say it.” For one second she’s thirteen.

Then she’s the COO again. He watches it happen: the shoulders coming down, the eyes sliding a little to the left, where she keeps her spreadsheets. He watches her decide what this is worth — to the board, to Monday, to the year. “Thank you,” she says. “I mean that.” She does. That’s the problem.

choices.text: Offer a truce. Split it before it splits you.
choices.ledger: You offered Hadley a truce. She said no.
response: “Here’s the thing,” he says. “What if we don’t? Do the Trial, either of us. What if we just split it? You run it. I wave. Co-heirs. Like the Mavericks, but with an adult in the owner’s box.”

She actually laughs. It surprises both of them; it comes out of her like a cough, and the bartender looks up. “That is the most Ransome thing you have ever said.” She shakes her head, still laughing, and it isn’t kind, but it isn’t cruel either. It’s worse. It’s accurate. “You’d give away half a company to get out of one fight. You’d give away the whole thing to get out of two.”
She slides off the stool. “No, Golden.”

s08b.slug: INT. THE ITALY — THE TWELVE-CAR GARAGE — NIGHT
body: The twelve-car garage in the Italy has a chandelier. Everyone who sees it for the first time says so, out loud, in the same voice — the garage has a chandelier — and then waits for someone to explain, and nobody ever does. It hangs over the polished concrete like a joke told to the cars: a Bentley Bentayga in a gray the dealer called Glacier; his father’s 1966 Lincoln Continental, black, suicide doors, the car Amon drove to his own first wedding; and Colt’s Raptor, wrapped bumper to bumper in a Mercy Ranch Water decal, MADE WITH SAN ISIDRO SPRING WATER, so that from the side it looks like a $9.99 four-pack with a lift kit.

Whit sits on the Lincoln’s back bumper with his phone face down on his knee. It buzzes. It buzzes again. Greer, Greer, Greer, a bar of light under his palm each time. On a workbench by the door a valet has left his own phone charging, still on Colt’s stream with the sound down to a mosquito: applause, the band, a man laughing, Colt saying something with the word content in it. Through a hundred feet of stucco, the Ball goes on without him, every bit as well.
