body.text: Greer’s napkin got most of the caliche off his cuffs. Not all of it. He looks at what’s left in the chandelier light, a pale chalk ghost on black wool. Six hundred people in that tent tonight, and he’d bet the Lincoln he’s the only one with any dirt on him.

body: The side door opens and lets in a slice of noise and a woman. The cane comes first, tapping on concrete, a sound with opinions. Then Lorna Whitaker Ransome: silver chignon, Chanel jacket over jeans, the cream cashmere wrap she wears in all weathers because she has been cold, she says, since 2009. She doesn’t hurry. She has never in her life hurried toward anything she could make come to her.

“I’ve walked out of better parties, darling,” his mother says. “I walked out of this marriage.” She considers the Bentley, then sits on its hood and arranges the wrap around her, as if it were a bench at MoMA in front of a painting she’d lent them.
She looks up at the chandelier. “Baccarat,” she says. “I chose it. In a garage.” She sounds faintly pleased with herself. “1998 was a very confident year.”

body.text: “Greer says your father had a dizzy spell,” she says, examining a nail. So Greer has already called his mother. Somewhere between the old hall and the speech, between Kilgore’s horse and the next thing, Greer found ninety seconds to brief Lorna. Whit files it with everything else he has filed tonight. The drawer is getting full.

body: “I’m practicing radical honesty, darling,” she says. “On you.” It has been her favorite line since she got sober; she says it the way other women say bless your heart. “You were right to leave. You were wrong to be seen leaving. Those are two different sins, and only one of them is any of my business, and it’s the second one.”
“Everyone saw, Mom.”

“Forty-one thousand people saw, I’m told. Colt texted me the number. With an emoji.” She taps the cane on the concrete once: a period. “Eleven years sober. I can smell a lie on a man the way I used to smell vodka, and I could smell it on that whole tent. Not on you. You’re the only one who left.”

Then her voice changes. It goes soft and goes back, the voice she uses at parties just before she tells it. “You always were the gentle one.” She reaches over and smooths his hair off his forehead, as if he were nine and running a fever. “You remember. You shot at that coyote and missed it by a mile, and you cried and cried. Your daddy was so mad, because you could have hit the horses. And you never would touch a gun again. Not once.” She smiles at something over his shoulder. “I wasn’t mad.”

Whit has heard it a hundred times. At Christmas, at the Stock Show, at his own rehearsal dinner, where it got a toast. He smiles at it the way you smile at a framed photo in a hallway you pass every day: fondly, and without really looking.

body.text: Except that when she says coyote, something else answers, from nowhere: Stay in the truck. His father’s voice. The grip on his wrist behind the barn. He doesn’t know why the two are in the same room in his head. They just are, for a second, side by side, like strangers who’ve stepped into the same elevator. He doesn’t mention it. It goes.

body: Lorna lets the story settle. Then, lightly, as if she were recommending a restaurant: “You know about my nine percent.” He knows. Everyone knows. It was the most expensive paragraph in the history of Texas family law: nine percent of Ransome Family Holdings, and with it a veto over any sale or merger. “Nobody sells this family out from under you,” she says. “Nobody merges you into some Midland vulgarian with turquoise on his boots. And nobody gets crowned, darling, without first wondering very hard what I think.” The cane taps. “Let me help you.”

She doesn’t name a price. She never does. With his mother, not knowing is the price: the bill that arrives years later in an envelope you’d forgotten you were expecting, with her handwriting on it, and a little drawing of a heart.

choices.text: Let her help. Owe her.
choices.ledger: You let your mother help. You owe her one.
response: “Okay,” he says. “Help.”

His mother pats his cheek twice, the way she used to pat it before school pictures. “Good boy. Go back in. Stand next to Soren in the photograph. Look like a man who stepped out to take a call from Austin: somebody important, a little annoying, you’ll tell the story later.”

She gets up off the Bentley, gathers her wrap and takes his arm for the walk across the lawn, as if he were escorting her and not the other way round. She’ll be in the photograph too, of course. She’s already arranging her face for it.

choices.text: Ask her what it costs.
choices.ledger: You asked your mother what her help would cost.
response: “What does it cost?”
Lorna looks at him with real interest, as if a painting she’d hung years ago had turned its head.

“A seat at the head table at the futurity,” she says, ticking them off on her rings. “My name back on the Ball. Lorna Whitaker Ransome, founding chair, in the program, above the fold. And to see your father’s face when you win.” She smiles, all honey. “I’m cheap, darling. That’s what the divorce lawyers said. Right up until they weren’t.”

choices.text: Ask about the coyote. Does she ever tell it when you’re not there?
choices.ledger: You asked your mother about the coyote.
response: “Do you ever tell it when I’m not there? The coyote?” He’s teasing her. He means it fondly.
“Every Christmas,” Lorna says, and laughs, and the laugh is perfect.

Then she’s quiet. Not for long: a second, maybe, one second too long, fixing the fall of the wrap over her shoulder, smoothing it, smoothing it again though it doesn’t need smoothing. Somewhere in the ductwork the air handler kicks on, and the chandelier ticks faintly overhead.

“Do you know what they wanted for that thing?” she says, looking up at it. “In 1998? I could have bought a Calder.” And she’s off: the chandelier, the decorator from Houston, the year everybody had money. Whit sits on the bumper of his father’s car and listens to his mother talk about light fixtures, which is something he has done his whole life, and doesn’t think about the coyote again.

s09.slug: EXT. THE MERCY BALL — THE STAGE APRON — NIGHT
body: 10:45. The photographer arranges the money.

She’s from Austin, she has shot two governors and a Kardashian wedding, and she arranges the money the way a good hand arranges a pen: by weight, by temperament, by who’s likely to kick. Amon at the center, on the lip of the stage. Soren Vale at his right, holding the blessed pipe across his chest in its white satin bow like a man who has been handed a baby and told it’s valuable. Pastor Jimmy Don Quick on Amon’s left, then Hadley, then Whit. At the far end, Kilgore and Deacon. “Horse’s good side is the left,” says the horse’s handler, a young woman in a RIDE FOR THE BRAND fleece who has signed a nondisclosure agreement about the horse and gives every sign of taking it seriously.

body.text: His phone lit up halfway across the lawn: Photo. Now. Or I have Colt film you hiding in a garage. He’s late. The line has already been built without him, and when he steps up onto the apron it opens a gap at the end and closes around him like water, and the photographer says “Perfect” without looking up.

His mother came across the lawn on his arm and let go of it at the apron, and by the time the photographer turns around Lorna has inserted herself between Soren and the pastor and is telling Soren about Rothko. “Mark would have adored your little data center. All that hum. He wanted people to weep in front of the paintings, and you want them to weep in front of the power bill.” “That’s so generous,” Soren says. The photographer moves a light stand eighteen inches to make room for her and doesn’t ask who she is. Nobody has ever had to ask.

body: Paloma stands at Amon’s elbow, half a step behind him, where the photographer has placed no one. Her face is arranged for the picture — pleasant, opaque, a face you could hang in a lobby — and from three bodies down Whit can see what the camera can’t. Her right hand is flat at the small of his father’s back, under the tux jacket, and it isn’t resting there. It’s holding. Every time the old man sways, a degree, less than a degree, the hand takes it, and Amon Ransome stands straight on her palm like a corner post on a brace. Six hundred people, eleven directors, a camera on a gimbal, and nobody sees it but Whit.

body.text: She doesn’t look at him once. Not when he steps up, not when the first flash goes.

Greer stands just off the end of the apron, outside the frame, one body-width closer to his father than protocol requires: close enough to catch him if it came to that, and to be photographed catching him. Insurance, in camel silk.

Beside him, Hadley watches their father’s left hand through the whole photograph — the pocket, the shape inside the pocket — exactly the way Greer would. Ten minutes ago she didn’t know to look. Now she can’t stop.
Beside him, Hadley smiles for the camera like a woman being deposed, and doesn’t look his way once.

body: Soren is delighted by everything. He is delighted by the pipe, by the pastor, by the horse, by the word caliche, which he learned tonight and has used four times. He asks the photographer if the pipe could be “a little more hero.” He tells Amon the aquifer is “basically a legacy liquidity event,” and Amon looks at him the way he’d look at a calf born with an extra leg: with real interest, and no plans to keep it. Then Soren gazes out past the tent at the dry black country running off forever under the stars and says, with total sincerity, “Is there a way to make the drought optional?” Nobody answers. Soren takes that as a yes.

He wants authentic family voices for the sizzle reel. Kilgore, who has been asked nothing, answers anyway, one hand on Deacon’s withers: “At the end of the day, Soren, this is about the values of rural Texas.” He laughs, and keeps laughing a little after the laugh is finished. In front of the line the handler crouches and holds up a laminated card to the horse that says SMILE. “Senator Deacon,” Whit says, under his breath, and the pastor pretends not to hear.

“And the village,” Soren says, turning in his new boots, which squeak. “The downstream one. The one with the feelings. Where is that, exactly? For the reel. We want to be super transparent about the geography.” Hadley opens her mouth — Hadley knows the acre-feet, the well logs, the district maps, she could draw them on a napkin — and Paloma, at Amon’s elbow, without turning her head, says: “Four miles downstream. Past the dead pecans.”

Amon looks at her. Hadley looks at her. It’s very quick, two heads turning a quarter-inch, and then the photographer says “Big smiles, the pipe’s drooping,” and it’s gone. Whit has been coming to the Mercy for thirty-three years and has never once driven that road. San Isidro is a sign he passes. Paloma, apparently, reads the whole contract.

Then Colt is in front of the line, walking backward, phone up on its gimbal and the GoPro on his hat brim blinking red like a second opinion. “Real quick for the stream, real quick, y’all —” Forty-some thousand people in the corner of his screen. “Whit. Cousin. Future — whatever, TBD. What’s Wellspring mean to you?”

Everyone waits. Soren waits with the joy of a man about to receive content. The pastor waits with his hands folded on his belt buckle. His father doesn’t turn his head, but Whit can feel him wait. At the end of the apron the photographer lowers her camera, because she has been doing this a long time and she knows that sometimes the picture is the face just before the answer.

dossier.text: Bought his Luccheses the day before the Ball. Asked if the drought could be made optional.
Knew the way to the downstream village better than anyone in the family.

choices.text: ‘Jobs. Four hundred of them. Pardee needs this.’
choices.ledger: You told Colt’s camera Wellspring means four hundred jobs.
response: “Jobs,” he says. “Four hundred of them. Pardee needs this.” He means it. He has at least driven through Pardee, past the two Dollar Generals competing for the same nine dollars, past the boarded Western Auto, and the line comes out sounding like the truth because mostly it is. Somebody behind Colt whoops. Kilgore says “Amen to that” and laughs a little past the amen.
When the flash goes, his father’s hand comes up and finds his shoulder and stays there two seconds after the light has died. Two seconds. In Amon Ransome, that’s a parade.
Down the line Paloma isn’t looking at the camera. She’s looking past the tent, into the dark, south, where the road goes.

choices.text: ‘Ask the village.’
choices.ledger: On camera, you said: ask the village.
response: “Ask the village,” Whit says. He doesn’t know he’s going to say it until it’s out, and then it’s out, on forty thousand phones, and he can’t find a joke to put after it, so for once he doesn’t.

A silence opens up the size of the tent. In it, a horse shifts its weight. Soren recovers first, because Soren always recovers first; it’s the only thing they teach in California. “Love that. Love that. Very community-forward.”
Amon’s face doesn’t change. It closes, the way a gate closes. Down the line Paloma turns her head and looks at him, really looks, as if she were seeing something she hadn’t bet on.
Hadley, beside him, through her photograph smile: “Golden. What the fuck.”

choices.text: ‘It means everybody wins, Soren. That’s the Texas miracle.’
choices.ledger: You told the stream that everybody wins.
response: “Here’s the thing,” Whit says, and finds Soren with the smile from the Christmas card. “It means everybody wins. That’s the Texas miracle.”

Soren puts a hand flat on his own heart. “Can we use that? Can we put that on the pipe?” He means it literally. He’s already looking at the pipe as if measuring it for letters. “Clipped, bro,” Colt says, reverent, and the little hearts go up the side of his screen like bubbles in a glass.
Across the line Hadley catches Whit’s eye and mouths one word at him, slowly, so he can’t possibly miss it: everybody.

s10.slug: INT. THE ITALY — JUNE’S ROOM — NIGHT
body: 10:58. The family wing of the Italy is the quietest place on the ranch, because a man from Houston was paid to make it that way: triple-glazed windows, a sound-baffled stairwell, a hall carpet so deep it eats footsteps. By the top of the stairs the Ball is just a hum in the window glass. Whit stands outside his daughter’s door for a second and takes his face off.

June’s room has a canopy bed nobody asked for. A designer from Highland Park chose it — four posts, a cloud of white voile, a price with its own payment schedule — and explained to Greer that a little girl needs “a place to feel sovereign.” Above it, on the wall, is a decal of a longhorn wearing a tiara. June chose that. It’s the only thing in the room she likes as much as her boots, which are on her feet right now, pink, under a white nightgown printed with horses, because she is waiting for fireworks, and you can’t wait for fireworks in bare feet. Everybody knows that.

She’s at the window with her nose flattened on the glass. Ximena sits on the window seat beside her in a battered UTEP hoodie, legs folded under her, a rubber-banded brick of LSAT flashcards in her lap. She looks up when Whit comes in and then back down, which is Ximena for good evening.

“Daddy.” June doesn’t turn around. She’s on duty. “A horse can’t throw up.” “Is that right.” “It can’t. Its stomach has a door that only goes one way. So if it eats something bad it just has to —” she looks for the word — “deal with it.” “That’s rough.” “And a Greenland shark can live four hundred years. It was alive when there were pilgrims.”

Whit sits down on the carpet beside the window seat in his tuxedo — the knees will never recover, and Greer will notice at breakfast — and does the Greenland shark, which is a very slow voice from the bottom of the sea that has seen everything and isn’t impressed. “I… remember… the pilgrims. They… were… rude.” June shrieks. He does the horse, who cannot throw up and is furious about it. He does the horse and the shark meeting at a gala. This is the one room in Texas where he isn’t doing a bit. He’s doing voices; that’s different.

body.text: “Cousin Colt said you got snubbed,” June tells the glass. “What’s snubbed?” Ximena’s flashcards stop moving. “I turned it off when I saw it, Mr. Ransome.” “I know you did.” He thinks about how to say it. “Snubbed is when somebody doesn’t pick you for something, in front of a lot of people.” June considers this. “Did you cry?” “No. I went and sat in the garage.” She nods, as if that’s the same thing. It sort of is.

“Cousin Colt said you said you test well,” June announces, proud of him. “I test well. I know all my sharks.” She proves it — mako, hammerhead, whale shark, which isn’t a whale, Greenland — and he listens to every one as if it were the best toast he’s ever heard. By some distance, it is.

“Everybody stood up for Grandpa,” June says. “And you stood up first. Ximena showed me.” Ximena, to her flashcards: “It seemed like the part she should see.” Whit doesn’t trust his voice, so he squeezes June’s ankle above the pink boot instead.
June puts her hand in his without looking, the way she does, as if he were a banister. He notices his own hand is steady now. An hour ago, behind the barn, it wasn’t. He doesn’t know when it stopped.

body: Out the window, across the dark lawn, the old House sits low and long under its tin roof, the 1928 limestone that the Italy was wrapped around in 1998 like a fur coat over work clothes. Two windows are lit in it, one at each end, a long way apart: the old room, where his father sleeps, and all the way down at the far east end, the blue room. June has her nose on the glass and she’s looking at them.
“Daddy,” she says. “Why does Grandpa’s wife sleep in the blue room and Grandpa sleeps in the old room?”
Ximena turns a flashcard over. She doesn’t look up.

Whit looks at Ximena, because she’s the nearest adult and he would like very much for this to be her question. Ximena feels it. She doesn’t raise her eyes from the card. “I don’t gossip, Mr. Ransome,” she says. “I document.”

Then, deadpan, reading, while down on the stock tank three men in headlamps pole a fireworks barge into position on the water the cattle drink: “Adverse possession. Open, notorious, continuous.” She flips the card to check herself. “And hostile,” she says. “I always forget hostile.”

June is still waiting. She’s five; she can wait for an answer longer than anyone on the board. Her breath makes a small fog on the glass, and in the fog her finger draws a horse, or a shark, or a horse meeting a shark.

choices.text: Tell her the truth: you don’t know. Stay till she’s asleep.
choices.ledger: You told June you didn’t know, and stayed until she slept.
response: “I don’t know, Junebug.” It’s the truest thing he has said all night, and the easiest.
“Okay,” June says. She sounds exactly like Paloma when she says it — the same flat, complete, unhurried okay, a whole sentence in two syllables — and he notices, and puts it somewhere.

She climbs into his lap to wait for the fireworks and is asleep before the first shell, mouth open, one fist wound into his lapel, pink boots still on. He takes them off one at a time, which is a two-person job with a sleeping five-year-old, and Ximena holds the second boot so it won’t thump. He carries June to the sovereign bed and puts her under the cloud.
He’s late for the fireworks. He doesn’t care.

choices.text: Make it funny. Grandpa snores like a longhorn.
choices.ledger: You told June Grandpa snores like a longhorn.
response: “Because Grandpa,” Whit says gravely, “snores like a longhorn.” And he does the longhorn: a long, rattling, nasal bellow he has been perfecting since he was June’s age, the one that used to make Tack laugh out loud in the barn, which nothing else did.
June shrieks and falls off the window seat into his lap. Ximena smiles at a flashcard about easements. June laughs until she gets the hiccups, satisfied.
Then, a little later, not quite: “But does he?”
He kisses the top of her head, where her hair smells like the strawberry detangler Greer buys by the case, and says goodnight, and goes down.

choices.text: Ask her what else she’s noticed.
choices.ledger: You asked your five-year-old what else she’d noticed.
response: “What else have you noticed?” June turns around from the window, thrilled. Nobody ever asks for her findings.

“Grandpa’s wife goes for walks at night,” she reports. “When we sleep over. To the church.” She points west, into the dark where the chapel is. “And she takes her shoes off at the door. Like it’s a house. She told me.”

Whit saw the shoes. Black satin, side by side inside the back door, heels to the wall. He says nothing. “You should be asleep when we sleep over,” he says, “not looking out windows,” and June says, “You asked,” which is fair.
Ximena, very quietly, without looking up: “She’s five, Mr. Ransome.” “She’s a better witness than I am.” Ximena turns over a flashcard. “That’s what worries me.”

s11.slug: EXT. THE SOUTH LAWN — THE FIREWORKS — NIGHT
body: 11:15. Six hundred people come out of the tent onto the south lawn with their drinks and stand in the dark facing southeast, toward the stock tank and the water tower, the way people in this part of Texas have always stood to face weather. The band has been moved onto a flatbed. The flatbed plays a country cover of “How Great Thou Art,” slow, heavy on the pedal steel, and the first thing to go up isn’t a firework. It’s a drone swarm: four hundred small lights lifting off the far bank of the stock tank in total silence and drawing the R-Bar-M across the sky, a hundred feet wide. The lawn says oh, the way it’s been paid to.

The brand dissolves and becomes the Ransome Horizon pronghorn, mid-leap, which gets applause. Then the pronghorn comes apart and the lights spell, in capitals across the whole southeast sky, HORZION. For one full second it hangs there. Then two drones swap places with a little apologetic hop and it reads HORIZON, and everyone claps harder, as if correcting yourself in public were the trick.

body.text: Whit comes down the Italy’s loggia stairs at a run as the drones go dark, tie flapping, and slides in beside Greer on the lawn. “You missed the brand.” “I was with June.” Her face softens a full degree, which on Greer is a lot of degrees. “Good,” she says, and takes his arm. Then, because she is Greer: “You also missed a hundred and eighty thousand dollars spelling Horizon wrong.”
body.else: Greer has his arm. She has had it since the drones went up, and under the hymn she’s reading him the vendor’s invoice off her phone. “A hundred and eighty thousand dollars. Four minutes. That’s seven hundred and fifty dollars a second, Whit.” The sky says HORZION. “It had better spell.”

body: A few bodies down the line his father stands upright and magnificent in the dark, hat on, chin up, like a general reviewing a parade of his own money. Paloma is at his side. Whit can’t see her hand, and he knows exactly where it is.

Then the first shell goes off over the stock tank, and Whit flinches — hard, all of him at once — and turns it in the same motion into a laugh, because he has never liked that sound and has never once said so.

After that it’s beautiful, the way money is beautiful when it’s set on fire on purpose. Gold willows over the stock tank, doubled in the black water. Red peonies. A white crossette that breaks into crosses, which Pastor Quick points out to everyone near him. Colt’s camera on the flatbed swings between the sky and the faces, and the forty-foot LED wall, towed out onto the lawn on a trailer, shows the faces looking at the sky, so that six hundred people can watch themselves being amazed. The hymn swells. The finale goes up in one long crackling roar like a grass fire in a high wind, and the whole south lawn is gold for eight seconds, and then the smoke drifts off toward Pardee and it’s 11:22 and it’s over, and everybody claps for the dark.
And the water tower lights up.

It stands where it has always stood, to the southeast, white, a hundred and forty feet high, the R-Bar-M painted on the tank in black. Now it’s glowing. A projection hits it square from somewhere out past the east fence, past the county road, and in letters twenty feet tall it says: RANSOME WATER = STOLEN WATER.

The crowd laughs. Of course it does; it looks like part of the show. Then somebody works it out and boos — a big, cheerful Midland boo, the kind you give the other team’s band — and somebody yells “Get a job!” and somebody else yells back “They want ours!” and that gets the biggest laugh of all.
The image changes. OJO VIVO · SAN ISIDRO · EL AGUA ES DE TODOS. Less laughter. Some people don’t know what it says. Some people do, and don’t say.
Then it changes again.

It’s a photograph. Low resolution, in the colors of an early digital camera, too warm, a little green in the shadows: a young man, thirty or so, squinting into old sun and smiling at whoever is holding the camera — a smile he didn’t have time to get ready. A short-sleeved polo with some kind of patch on the chest. A clipboard held flat against him like he’s about to read from it. Under him, in plain white block capitals: ¿Y TEO?
Nobody laughs at that one.

Whit doesn’t know the face. He looks at it hard, and it’s nobody: a nice-looking stranger in a work shirt, twenty feet tall on the side of his family’s water tower, asking a question in Spanish that Whit can translate and can’t answer. And Teo? He turns to his wife, because Greer always knows who everybody is.

Greer has gone very still. Her reading glasses are in her hand, out of the case, unfolded, and she isn’t using them. She isn’t doing anything with them at all. She’s holding them and looking at the tower, and Whit, who has watched his wife in a thousand rooms, can’t remember ever seeing her hold a thing without using it.

He looks down the line. Paloma has gone still, all the way to the bottom, her eyes on the tower and her face nothing at all. She must be mortified: her husband’s tower, her husband’s name, six hundred people who already think she married a punchline. He feels for her.

His father is staring at the tower. Not angry. Not anything Whit has a word for. He is looking at the photograph the way he looked at the fence line behind the cutting barn: as if it had walked up to him and spoken. Whit sees it. He doesn’t let himself think it.

Tack is already moving. Whit catches him at the very edge of the light: the rented jacket, the reading glasses swinging on their string, walking the east fence toward the county road at an old man’s unhurried pace that eats ground like a good horse’s walk. Nobody sent him. Out on FM 2400, red and blue lights come on and start toward the east gate, small and silent across the distance.

body.text: That’s all it was, Whit thinks, watching him go. It’s the second time tonight Tack has walked toward something before anybody asked him to.
Behind Whit, low, a man’s voice, a donor’s, amused: “Ask the village, he says.” A glass lifted toward the tower. “There’s the village.”
Greer, without turning her head from the tower: “Your friend’s very quiet.” Whit looks for an answer to that, and there isn’t one anywhere.
Hadley isn’t watching the tower at all. She’s watching their father.

body: On the flatbed, Colt has the phone turned around on his own face, lit blue from below, and he’s talking fast and low the way he only does when something is real. “Okay. Okay. Y’all are seeing this. This is so bad for the brand.” His eyes flick to the corner of the screen, where the number is climbing like a pump-jack counter. “This is so good for engagement.” Ten feet away Bunny Ashworth is typing with both thumbs, and humming.
Up on the tower, the young man in the polo shirt goes on smiling at whoever was holding the camera.

dossier.text: Named no heir at the Mercy Ball. Put his children on trial for a year instead.

choices.text: Ask Greer who Teo is.
choices.ledger: You asked Greer who Teo was. She said nobody.
response: “Who’s Teo?”
Greer folds the glasses. Slides them into her clutch, snaps it shut. “Nobody,” she says. “A slogan. Smile — Colt’s filming.”

Her phone is already at her ear. Her voice drops into the register she used at Brightline, low and pleasant and perfect, a voice like a door closing on carpet: the county judge, then the sheriff, then somebody at the projection company’s insurer whose name she somehow already has. “I’ll have it down in four minutes,” she tells Whit, between calls.
It takes three. Out past the east fence a generator coughs and dies, and the young man on the tower goes out like a match.

choices.text: Look for Paloma. Just look.
choices.ledger: In the dark, you looked for Paloma. She was already looking back.
response: He doesn’t do anything. He just looks for her.

She’s looking at the tower. Then at his father, short, up and to the side, checking something. Then — across eleven people, two board wives, a pastor and a man holding a Mercy Ranch Water can like a grenade — at Whit.

She doesn’t look away. He doesn’t either. It goes on long enough to stop being an accident, and keeps going, until it’s a thing that has happened; and out past the east fence a generator coughs and the tower goes dark, and neither of them looks at the tower.
Behind them, Bunny Ashworth starts to hum.

choices.text: Walk toward the tower.
choices.cue: Tack saw which way you were walking.
choices.ledger: You walked toward the water tower. Tack turned you around.
response: He lets go of Greer’s arm — he’ll pay for that later, in some currency — and walks. Off the lawn, out of the light, into the hay stubble where the valets have parked the Escalades in long rows like cattle at a sale: two hundred yards of dark toward the east fence, the man on the tower getting bigger the whole way and no clearer.

At the wire he stops. Across the bar ditch, on the shoulder of FM 2400, a white box truck with its back door rolled up and a projector inside ticking hot. A generator. Two kids in hoodies coiling cable. And by the cab a woman in a sun-bleached cap with her arms folded, who looks at Whit across the fence — straight at him, once, a long, level, unhurried look with no fear in it anywhere, as if she’d been expecting somebody from the house and he’ll do.
She says something to the kids. The generator dies. The tower goes dark. The truck pulls away with its lights off, and the sheriff’s lights are still a mile up the road.

A hand on his elbow. He didn’t hear anyone come. “Leave it, Bud.” Tack, out of the dark, breathing a little from the walk. “Sheriff’s got it.” It’s gentle — the same voice that taught Whit to post a trot — and it doesn’t move, not an inch, until Whit turns around.

choices.text: Make a joke about the projector budget.
choices.ledger: You made a joke about the activists’ projector budget.
response: “Here’s the thing, Coltrane,” Whit says, loud enough for the flatbed. “Their projector’s nicer than ours.”

Colt howls. He actually howls, on the flatbed, on the stream, and swings the phone around to catch the end of it, and the people nearest them laugh like people who have finally been given permission. A board wife says “Oh, Whit,” fondly. Greer squeezes his hand once: good, that was the right size. Hadley doesn’t laugh.
And down the line Paloma doesn’t laugh either. Doesn’t turn, doesn’t do anything at all, and he notices: one empty chair at a full table.
Out past the fence a generator coughs, and the man on the tower goes dark in the middle of his smile.

s12.slug: EXT. THE HOUSE — THE OLD PORCH STEPS — LATE NIGHT
body: At 1:20 a.m. the Mercy Ball is a pallet of Mercy Ranch Water by the service tent, shrink-wrapped, unopened, twelve hundred cans of San Isidro spring water at $9.99 a four-pack going nowhere. Caterers in black are loading chafing dishes into a reefer truck. A valet is asleep at the wheel of an Escalade with his mouth open and the key fob on his chest. The ice brand has finished melting. In its silver tray there’s a puddle with an R in it.

Greer is awake in their suite in the Italy with her laptop on her knees, drafting a memo in a Google Doc titled TRIAL. When Whit left she was on page three and had built a table, and one of its columns was headed EXPOSURES. She looked up long enough to say “Don’t go far,” and went back to the table. Whit can’t sleep. He has never been able to sleep at the Mercy; he blames the quiet. So he walks, in the tux with the tie in his pocket, across the dead lawn and around the side of the old House, for no reason, which is the reason he gives himself.

She’s on the porch steps. The old part of the House, the 1928 limestone, with the tin roof and the screen door and a Scottie-dog bootscraper older than anyone alive. She’s sitting on the second step, barefoot, in the black dress, her shoes side by side on the step beside her like two small animals asleep. The chip is going over her knuckles. Behind her, through the screen and down the hall, the old room’s window is lit.

She isn’t waiting for him; that’s clear. She doesn’t seem surprised he came, either. She looks at him as if he were a hand she’d seen dealt and was waiting to see played. “Sit,” she says, “if you’re going to stand there,” and he sits, one step down and a careful distance over.

body.text: The shoes. Like it’s a house, June said. Whit looks at them lined up on the step and doesn’t ask what other doors she leaves them at.
Neither of them mentions the look across the lawn. It sits on the step between them like a third person who has been told to keep quiet.

body: For a while neither of them says anything. Out on the lawn the reefer truck’s door bangs shut. A coyote starts up somewhere south and gives it up. “Six hundred people,” Paloma says eventually, “paid twenty-five thousand dollars a table to watch your family be told it might lose.” The chip turns over. “Literacy’s going to be fine.”

Then she does something he’ll come to recognize: she goes back over the hands. Not the cards. The players — what they did, and when, and what it cost them. She does it quietly, without looking at him, like someone reading back a list of what was ordered.

body.text: “You called him Dad,” she says. “On your knees. In the dirt. Nobody’s called him that in a while, I think.”

“You were afraid he’d pick you,” she says. “He didn’t. How’s it feel?” He thinks about it honestly, which is rare enough at 1:20 in the morning that he notices himself doing it. “Like being let off a hook I was hanging from by the face.” “Okay.”
“You kept it,” she says. “It’s only been four hours.” “That’s a long time, in your family.”

“You told her.” It isn’t a question. Whit starts to explain, and she shakes her head a quarter-inch, not unkindly. “I’d have told her too,” she says. “I’d have lied about it better.” There’s no anger in it anywhere, which leaves him nothing to push against.

“You told your sister.” He hasn’t said so. He looks at her. “She watched his hand all through the photograph,” Paloma says. “Nobody watches a hand unless somebody told them where to look.” He doesn’t ask how she noticed. She notices everything, he is beginning to understand, and it costs her nothing, the way charm costs him nothing.
“You took my side in a hallway.” She says it to the lawn. “Your wife will make you pay for that in installments.”
“You took your wife’s side at the door. That was right.” She means it. He can hear that she means it, and he would have preferred almost anything else.
“Ask the village.” A look. “Have you ever been?” “No.” “Okay.”

Somewhere in the middle of it Whit realizes he never saw the old room tonight. Tack drove his father away and Paloma went with him, and she was in there with the old man the whole time Whit was on the lawn being charming. He doesn’t know what that room looks like with his father hurt in it. She does.
“You walked out,” she says. “Everyone thinks it was weak.” “Was it?” “It was early. You folded a hand you hadn’t looked at.” The chip turns over. “Sometimes that’s right.”
“‘I’ve always tested well.’” She does his voice a little. It isn’t bad. “They laughed. Your father didn’t.” “He never does.” “He did once.” The chip goes over and back. “In Midland. At me.”
“You stood up first,” she says. “For him.” “Somebody had to.” The chip turns over. “Nobody had to.”
“And you still owe me,” she says, last, like closing out a tab.

body: Then she asks him something, and he understands while she’s asking it that she doesn’t need the answer. She just wants to watch him look for one. “When he said I’m not going to,” she says, “what was the first thing you felt? Not the second thing. The first.” He opens his mouth. She’s already looking away, up at the lit window behind them.

body.text: The chip walks over her knuckles, first finger to little finger and back, red and worn and older than she is. Then, without any ceremony at all, she reaches down and rolls it once across the backs of his — four knuckles, cool clay, five thousand dollars — and takes it back before he can close his hand. That’s all. It’s the lightest anyone has touched him all night, and the only time he’s held still for it.
body.else: The chip walks over her knuckles, first finger to little finger and back, red and worn and older than she is. Then she sets it on the step between them, face up, and leaves it there a moment, as if showing him the stake, not offering it. Then she takes it back.

choices.text: Give her your jacket. Don’t make it a moment.
choices.ledger: You gave Paloma your jacket on the House steps. She didn’t give it back.
response: He takes off the tux jacket, warm from him, two index cards still in the breast pocket, and puts it around her shoulders. He doesn’t say anything. He doesn’t make it anything. He sits back down a careful foot away.

She doesn’t say thank you. She pulls it closed at the throat with one hand, the chip still in her fist. After a while she stands, picks up her shoes and goes in wearing it, and the screen door eases shut behind her on its old spring.

choices.text: Ask her who Teo is.
choices.ledger: You asked Paloma who Teo was. She asked you back.
response: “Who’s Teo?” She doesn’t stop the chip. “Why would I know?” “You went still. At the tower.” “I go still a lot.” Over and back. “It’s a habit. It’s a good one at a table.”

Then she turns it around on him, smoothly, the way a card comes off the bottom of a deck: “Who do you think he is?” He has no idea. He says so. He says it twice, actually, and puts a joke on the end of it, and she lets the joke go by and watches him not know, closely and steadily, as she’d watch a man’s hands at a table. Whatever she’s looking for, he can’t tell whether she finds it.
“Goodnight, Whit.” She picks up her shoes and goes in, and leaves the screen door standing open behind her. After a while the night swings it shut.

response: He stands, and buttons his jacket, and says it. “Goodnight, Mrs. Ransome.” It’s the right thing. It’s a line drawn on purpose, in the dirt, and he watches her watch him draw it.
“Goodnight, Mr. Ransome.” The formality is louder than anything either of them has said all night. It comes back off the limestone like a shot off a canyon wall.
She gathers her shoes and goes in, and lets the screen door slap.

“No,” she says. “Everybody in that tent had the second thing.” The chip turns over. “Okay.”

s12b.slug: EXT. THE HOUSE — THE OLD PORCH STEPS — LATER
body: Whit stays on the step. Out on the lawn the reefer truck pulls away with the last of the chafing dishes, and the pallet of Ranch Water stays where it is.

Through the screen and down the hall, the old room’s light goes out. A minute later — he counts, without meaning to — a light comes on at the far east end of the House, in the blue room, a long way from the first.

body.text: He sits there in his shirtsleeves and looks at the two windows, the dark one and the lit one, until the cold gets into the step.

s13.slug: INT./EXT. THE CHAPEL AT THE MERCY — 3:10 A.M.
body: 3:10 a.m. A 2004 Silverado comes along the chapel road with its lights off and stops on the gravel by the west wall. The engine ticks as it cools. Nothing else on two hundred thousand acres makes a sound.

body.text: Tack sits behind the wheel with the engine off and doesn’t get out. A minute. Longer.
On the dash, beside the Thermos, lies a flyer someone tucked under his wiper while the truck sat by the service tent. OJO VIVO. He has folded it in quarters, printed side in.

body: He gets out. He has traded the rented jacket for a canvas chore coat, and the pearl snaps are done up to the throat. He takes a flashlight from the door pocket and walks the outside of the west wall along the gravel drip bed, slowly, beam low, the way you walk a fence looking for the place where something got through.

Three orange flags on wire stakes stand in a line through the gravel and on out toward the lawn, bright as candy in the light. Black printing on the vinyl. HALCYON / WELLSPRING ROW — STA 14+50. The next: STA 14+75. The next: STA 15+00. He pulls the first one out of the gravel and wraps the wire twice around two fingers, neat, the flag folded inside the coil, and puts it in his shirt pocket. Then the second. Then the third. He shines the flashlight on along the line, out over the grass, to where the next one would be, and moves the beam slowly back and forth. There isn’t one. He keeps looking anyway.

Inside, he doesn’t turn on the lights. The chapel smells of cedar and lemon oil and the last of somebody’s lilies. The beam goes up the center aisle ahead of him, over a hundred and twenty empty seats, and finds the front pew, and on the front pew a white index card lying face down. He picks it up. Turns it over. Thank you, Dad, for — in blue ink, crossed out twice. He reads it for longer than it takes to read. Then he puts it in his shirt pocket with the flags and snaps the pocket shut.

He steps up onto the altar step, at the west end, where the couples stand. He stands there. He doesn’t kneel. He looks down at the polished cedar under his boots in the circle of the flashlight, and the beam doesn’t move. Up in the eaves a great horned owl shifts its weight and settles.
“Well,” Tack says.

His phone buzzes in his coat. He takes it out, and the screen lights his face from below — the white mustache, the glasses on their string. A text, from a contact saved as A.: Is he still out there. No question mark.
Tack crosses to the west window and looks out. Past the gravel, past the lawn, the pasture runs off into the dark to the fence line, a long pale wire under no moon. There is nothing there.
He types with one thumb, slowly, the way he does everything. No sir. Go to sleep.

Then he walks back down the aisle without the flashlight, and sits down in the back pew, at the end, in the place where Amon sits when he comes here. He sets his hat on the seat beside him. The window goes gray.
